utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is our expectation that with the earlier start and focused presentations, we may - without prejudicing the rights of any party - conclude the proceedings today. We may take an abbreviated lunch break. Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For the record, my name is Peter Kremer, I appear on behalf of the Prosecution. With me this morning is Mr. Paul Rogers and Mr. Kyle Wood, who you are familiar with from earlier submissions. Let me begin by briefly outlining how the Prosecution will present its oral arguments on its appeal. We will use the order of the response submissions and the length of our submissions as a guide. As such, I will make very brief submissions concerning Beara and Popovic's acquittal for conspiracy to commit genocide and Miletic's acquittal for murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. These are grounds 6 and 9 of our appeal respectively. Mr. Rogers will then make submissions concerning Drago Nikolic's erroneous acquittal for conspiracy to commit genocide, ground 7 of our appeal, as well as answer your question relating to those issues. We rely on our submissions as to why Nikolic's sentence was manifestly inadequate, and that is ground 8 of our appeal. But as I say, we rely on our written submissions for the adequacy for that appeal. Mr. Wood and I will then conclude by making submissions concerning Vinko Pandurevic. Mr. Wood will answer questions ii, iii, iv, and v, and in doing so will present our submissions on ground 2, his superior responsibility under Article 7(3). I will speak to ground 1, which challenges the Trial Chamber's findings regarding his criminal responsibility under Article 7(1), and I will only address grounds 1(A) and 1(B). For subground 1(C), we rely on our brief. Time permitting, Mr. Wood will make a few short remarks about ground 3, Pandurevic's manifestly inadequate sentence. As Your Honours are well aware, grounds 4 and 5 are moot given Mr. Gvero's passing. And as for remedy, the Prosecution refers Your Honours to the prayers for relief found in both our notice of appeal and appeal brief. Starting with ground 6, our appeal against Beara and Popovic's acquittal for conspiracy to commit genocide. We observe that on 9 October 2012, the ICTR Appeals Chamber in Gatete decided the issue of cumulative convictions for conspiracy to commit genocide and genocide. And I refer to those findings in the appeals judgement at paragraphs 259 to 264. Like the Trial Chamber in Gatete, the Trial Chamber in this case found Popovic and Beara criminally responsible for genocide and for conspiracy to commit genocide but only convicted them of genocide. The Gatete appeal judgement, Judge Agius dissenting, found that the Trial Chamber erred in law by failing to hold Gatete responsible for the totality of his criminal conduct, which included entering into the unlawful agreement to commit genocide, just as the Prosecution has argued in ground 6. The Gatete Appeals Chamber expressly disagreed with the Trial Chamber's reliance on the Popovic Trial Chamber's reasoning for declining to enter a cumulative conviction. In particular, the Appeals Chamber concluded that, one, the danger represented by the agreement to commit genocide itself justifies punishing the acts of conspiracy, even where the substantive crime has been committed; and two, it is the legal elements of two crimes that must be compared to determine whether they are permissibly cumulative, not the underlying evidence. The Gatete appeals judgement fully supports the Prosecution's arguments in ground 6 and confirms that the Popovic Trial Chamber took an erroneous approach. The Gatete Appeals Chamber provided a thorough analysis of the issue which is highly persuasive and should be followed by this Chamber. Unless there are questions from the Bench on this ground, we have no further submissions. Turning to ground 9, Miletic's acquittal for murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, all of the elements required to convict Miletic of this crime were established. The Chamber convicted Miletic of these killings under JCE 3, but only for murder as a crime against humanity and as an underlying act of persecution, but not as a war crime. The Chamber reasoned in paragraph 1727, and I quote: "... that in the circumstances of 'opportunistic' killings arising from a JCE to forcibly remove - encompassing forcible transfer as other inhumane acts constituting a crime against humanity - his criminal responsibility is for murder as a crime against humanity and not as a war crime." This finding is erroneous, regardless of whether the Chamber reached it as a factual or legal conclusion. If the Chamber meant that it is a legal requirement that the JCE 3 crime is to be of the same category, that is, a crime against humanity, as the JCE 1 crime, then it is wrong in law. As we have set out in our appeal brief, the Appeals Chamber in Stakic and Martic affirmed convictions for murder as a war crime under JCE 3, although the JCE 1 crime was a crime against humanity. And I refer you to our appeal brief at paragraph 325. If the Chamber meant that it could not conclude factually that murder as a war crime was a natural and foreseeable consequence of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly displace and that Miletic could foresee this and willingly took the risk, then this is an unreasonable conclusion. What distinguishes murder as a war crime under Common Article 3 from murder as a crime against humanity, is that the crime needs to be closely related to the armed conflict and that the victims are persons not taking part in the -- active part in the hostilities. On the facts of this case, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that it was not a natural and foreseeable consequence that murder closely related to the armed conflict would occur, given that part of the coercion used was a full-scale military attack on Srebrenica. Similarly, in light of the aim to remove the civilian population from Srebrenica, it was a natural and foreseeable consequence that persons not taking active part in the hostilities might be killed. In light of Miletic's role and involvement in the joint criminal enterprise and his intimate knowledge of the events, the only reasonable conclusion is that it was foreseeable to him personally that killings closely related to the armed conflict might occur in relation to victims not taking active part in the hostilities. Unless there are questions on this ground, I will now pass the podium to Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and my colleagues for the Defence and everyone else in and around the courtroom. Your Honours, I will be dealing with the appeal relating to Drago Nikolic, as Mr. Kremer has indicated. In relation to our remarks concerning conspiracy, we rely upon our brief and the arguments insofar as they are necessary relating to Gatete which Mr. Kremer has outlined. My submissions will be confined to answering Your Honours' two questions that you have posed to the parties, and of course in relation to question 2, and the submissions I would have made will be in relation to the appeal as a whole will be somewhat encompassed within. So I ask Your Honours to have regard to that, and for the rest we rely upon our brief. Your Honours, in relation to the question -- the first question that Your Honours ask: Discuss whether the Prosecution's allegation that the Trial Chamber failed to apply the accepted factors for inferring genocidal intent to the evidence when assessing Nikolic's mens rea for genocide exceeds the Prosecution's notice of appeal, and if it does, whether the Prosecution wishes to add any further arguments to its motion to vary its notice of appeal concerning good cause for variation. Your Honours, simply put, our submission is that the paragraphs that you've identified, 237 to 243, are not new arguments but are an aspect of the factual ground and, as such, are wrapped up in the error alleged in paragraph 39 of our notice of appeal. This is because the argument falls within the general factual error articulated in ground 7 of the notice and arguments detailing that error belong in the brief and not in the notice. Using factors that have been identified as evidential considerations from which genocidal intent can be inferred is one way to show that the Trial Chamber's assessment in this case was one that no reasonable Trial Chamber could make. Thus, it is an aspect of the factual error. Indeed, the whole of the Prosecution's appeal brief primarily is an explanation of the factual error. The only legal error identified in the notice of appeal concerns the assessment of legally irrelevant considerations, and the arguments relating to those are set out in paragraphs 274 and 285 to 288 of the brief. Everything else that is argued relates to the factual appeal because it relates to the assessment of the available evidence and the unreasonable conclusion of the Trial Chamber giving rise to a miscarriage of justice. The relevant factors referred to in 237 to 243 describe a number of facts and circumstances from which genocidal intent may be inferred. Those factors are also referenced in the judgement itself at paragraph 823 and 824. These arguments form part of the factual assessment error and properly appear in the brief, not the notice of appeal. And, Your Honours, we would refer you also to the decision in the Mrksic appeal dated the 26th of August, 2008, paragraph 8, cited in our reply brief. Your Honours, in our submission a broad pleading of a factual error will encompass all of the elements and all of the arguments that go to support how that error is made out. The Prosecution's argument here falls within the factual error pleaded in the notice of appeal, similarly to that in the Mrksic decision at paragraph 26, because it clearly addresses the single question, which is the mens rea aspect of Nikolic's responsibility which is the core of the Prosecution's submission under its seventh ground of appeal. Thus, our primary argument remains that we do not exceed the notice of appeal. However, should Your Honours reject that argument and consider the argument should have been separately articulated as a legal error, good cause exists for not including or articulating it as a legal error in the notice. Firstly, the line between legal and factual errors is not always clear in the jurisprudence. In some previous cases where the Prosecution has alleged errors regarding the assessment or relevant factual circumstances or factors as legal errors, the Appeals Chamber has recharacterised them as factual. For example, in the Naletilic appeals judgement, paragraph 128 and 139 to 140; also in Krnojelac appeals judgement, paragraph 187 to 202. Having regard to the Mrksic decision, in our submission it was reasonable to consider that the argument detailing the error should be made in the brief rather than in the notice. In addition to the reasons provided for good cause for variation in our reply brief, the Prosecution notes and submits that no unfair prejudice would result because Nikolic has fully responded to the arguments developed in the Prosecution's brief in his response brief. And in similar circumstances, we refer you again to the Mrksic decision, paragraph 37; the Nchamihigo appeals judgement paragraph 331; and the Blagojevic and Jokic appeals decision of the 20th of July, 2005. Your Honours, that said, I will pass, if I may, to the second question that Your Honours ask. Your Honours asked: Discuss whether in taking into account the alleged errors committed by the Trial Chamber in determining Nikolic's mens rea for genocide Nikolic's specific intent for genocide would be unequivocally established, and particularly whether genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. The answer is yes because the general context and all the other factors of scale and systematic targeting show that a genocide was being implemented. Indeed, the judgement found that the murder operation was genocidal because Nikolic was a party to the plan to murder with Popovic and Beara and shared their intent to kill and to exterminate; because Popovic and Beara were implementing the murder plan in order to commit genocide; because Nikolic knew that Popovic and Beara were murdering in order to further genocide, in the judgement at 1407; because the Chamber found Nikolic's main contributions to the murder plan were made concurrent with and after the acquisition of this knowledge, judgement 1407; because having joined the murder operation, knowing it was genocidal, Nikolic was "persistent and determined," judgement 1408; because he demonstrated resolve, 1409; because he pursued personnel for the executions at Rocevic, 1409; because he was actively involved in many of the facets of the operation at Orahovac, 1409; because he arranged the guarding of prisoners at the Kula school, 1409; because he was with Beara near the Petkovci school, judgement 498; and because he was disciplined, judgement 1413. The answer is yes because motive is irrelevant to the issue of specific intent. It is clear that the Trial Chamber were affected by considerations of motive when they determined mens rea was not proved at 1414, when they stated: "... another reasonable inference is that Nikolic's blind dedication to the security service led him to doggedly pursue the efficient execution of his assigned tasks in this operation, despite its murderous nature and the genocidal aim of his superiors ..." In other words, he was motivated by a sense of service or a desire to please, and thus he had no intent. This is simply irrelevant, as the Jelisic Appeals Chamber at paragraph 49, citing to the Tadic appeals judgement at 269 said: "The existence of a personal motive does not preclude the perpetrator from also having the specific intent to commit genocide." In the Tadic appeals judgement the Appeals Chamber stressed the irrelevance and inscrutability of motives in criminal law." And there follows in that paragraph in Tadic at 269 an interesting analysis of a reductio ad absurdum on this specific point relating to mass killing, and it's instructive to look at it but I won't read it out here in court. Your Honours, we also refer to the Kayishema appeals judgement at 161, the Niyitegeka appeals judgement at 53, Kvocka appeals judgement at 367 and 416. Your Honours, in the Duch appeals judgement -- we're just -- I'm aware of Your Honours and I want to make sure that Your Honours are able to follow. In the Duch appeals judgement on the 3rd of February, 2012, at paragraph 240, the ECCC Appeals Chamber spoke of motive in the context of persecution in this way, they said: "The specific motive out of which he engaged in the persecution, that is, whether he internalised the goals of the CPK behind the persecutory policy or only wanted to prove himself as a loyal and efficient member of the party is immaterial for finding he possessed the requisite specific intent." And in the Charles Taylor appeals judgement in the footnote at 1382, they explained that motive: "... concerns the extraneous reasons and motivations that triggered an accused to engage in criminal conduct." In the case of Drago Nikolic, the Trial Chamber relied upon these extraneous reasons and motivations in acquitting him. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber looked at Nikolic's personal circumstances at 1412, such as his rank, that he had not attended military academy, that he was chief of security, a post usually reserved for a higher rank, that he had little authority on his own, that he was brought in by others, that the order came from Mladic. But, Your Honours, to possess genocidal intent, he did not need to be a general or a colonel, or to be powerful or independent. He did not need to access the greatest of resources or to be competent or efficient or to take part in all of the aspects of the operation or even to do all that he can. Your Honours, Nikolic did not need to be an architect to be a genocidaire, as the Trial Chamber seemed to consider at 1410. Your Honours, the formation of genocidal intent is not precluded by being out of your depth, as the Trial Chamber seemed to consider at 1413, when it recorded Pandurevic's view that the cloak of the security service was much too big for him. None of these factors identified by the Chamber in 1412 or 1413 are ones which preclude the formation of a specific intent. Nikolic's position in the hierarchy simply goes to his ability to act. The fact his role was not as encompassing as that of Popovic or Beara does not stop him from having genocidal intent. To do so would be to confine genocide to those with the power to act or ability to act on a great or grand scale. As the Appeals Chamber in Kayishema held at judgement 170: "Genocide is not a crime that can only be committed by certain categories of person. As evidenced by history, it is a crime which has been committed by low-level executioner and high-level planner and instigator alike." To be a genocidaire, all that is required are actions, in this case killings, directed at members of the protected group, carried out with intent to destroy that group in whole or in part. Here those actions were carried out by Drago Nikolic with grim determination and steadfast resolve. He did not have to be passionate or enthusiastic. He may have been somber or angry or weak or eager to please. But once he chose to act and participate, in this case with resolve and determination, his genocidal intent is manifest by his actions. He knew the evil purpose, he possessed the same persecutory intent as Popovic and Beara. He knew what the killing was for, what it was aimed at, and he joined in. Whatever his motivation may have been, and is not relevant, the only reasonable conclusion is that Drago Nikolic possessed genocidal intent. And thus we answer Your Honours' question: Yes. Your Honours, that concludes the answer to those questions, and I will pass - unless Your Honours have questions - to Mr. Wood to conclude -- to continue with the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. In relation to ground 2 of the Prosecution appeal, I'll limit my remarks to addressing, as Mr. Kremer said, the second, third, fourth, and fifth questions on page 3 of the 6 November 2013 order for the preparation of the appeal hearing. With the possible exception of sentencing, time permitting, after Mr. Kremer's remarks. For those grounds of appeal that I don't address today, as ever, we continue to rely on our written submissions. So going straight away then to Your Honours' question 2 or discussion point 2, which is: Discuss the Trial Chamber's finding that Pandurevic did not have sufficient notice of the Zvornik Brigade's involvement in possible exterminations as of 12.00 p.m. on 15 July 1995. As we argue, Your Honours, in ground 2 of our appeal, the Chamber erred in law by finding that Pandurevic's duty to prevent was not triggered until he had found out concretely [Realtime transcript read in error "completely"] that his subordinates had already participated in 3.000 murders. Further, no reasonable Chamber could have concluded that Pandurevic did not [sic] know or have reason to know, at noon on 15 July, that his subordinates might participate in extermination under Article 7(3). So turning to the legal error first. I'll note that the Trial Chamber articulated, Your Honours, at paragraph 1038 the proper legal standard for determining when precisely a subordinate -- a commander's requirement or duty to prevent is triggered under Article 7(3). And the Chamber said: "The information required to put a superior on notice need not be specific. Rather, it must 'put him on notice of possible unlawful acts by his subordinates.'" Applying this standard, Your Honours, to the question of when Pandurevic's duty to prevent murder was triggered, the Chamber found that Pandurevic had reason to know that his subordinates might commit murder based on what he knew at around noon on 15 July 1995. And what is that knowledge? According to the Chamber, General Pandurevic knew that a large number of prisoners had been brought from Bratunac to the Zvornik sector. General Pandurevic knew that these prisoners were being executed. And General Pandurevic knew according to his subordinates that there were "enormous problems with the guarding, execution and burial of the prisoners." That's at trial judgement paragraphs 1861 and 2037. The Chamber also found that General Pandurevic knew that these prisoners were being killed as part of a plan to murder the able-bodied Bosnian Muslim males from Srebrenica. And that's the Chamber's finding at paragraph 1960. General Pandurevic also knew that this was causing "an additional burden" on his brigade, and that's at paragraphs 1870 and 1949 of the judgement. When it comes to extermination, however, the Chamber found that Pandurevic's duty to prevent wasn't triggered until he had acquired details of the actual numbers of prisoners killed, rather than reason to know his subordinates might commit murder on a mass scale. This is clear, Your Honours, from reading two specific paragraphs of the judgement. At paragraph 2070 [sic] of the judgement, the Chamber found that on the 18th of July, Pandurevic had "knowledge of the large-scale murders of the men and boys from Srebrenica ..." That is by the 18th of July. It cites to General Pandurevic's interim combat report of the 18th of July in which he refers to 3.000 Bosnian Muslim males having been brought to the area of Zvornik. Three paragraphs later, however, the Chamber implicitly contrasted this level of knowledge on the 18th of July with the "obvious limitations" of Pandurevic's knowledge on the 15th. And it found that his Article 7(3) responsibility was only triggered "at a late stage." Now, Your Honours, the only possible limitation the Chamber can be referring to is that on the 15th of July, unlike on the 18th of July, which was assuredly a late stage in the murder operation, Pandurevic didn't know that specifically 3.000 had been killed. Now, this is contrary, Your Honours, to the correct reason to know standard, as the Chamber properly articulated it and applied it to murder. In any event, Your Honours, as to the factual error, the characteristic of extermination is that in what distinguishes it from murder is scale. It is the killing of a large number of individuals, and this is at paragraph 800 of the trial judgement. No reasonable finder of fact could have concluded that Pandurevic did not know or have reason to know at noon on the 15th that his subordinates might participate in mass killings. Considering, as I've outlined, that he knew they were participating in a systematic murder operation of a number of -- a group of individuals that was so large that it was creating enormous problems with the guarding, execution, and burial, and it was so large that it was creating an additional burden for his brigade. Further, Your Honours, in this respect, remembering that this is a 7(3) case as to this part, Pandurevic need only have asked if he needed more information at noon on the 15th of July. Recall that he received this information from his Chief of Staff, Obrenovic. At that moment, he could have inquired further. He could have inquired of Nikolic. He could have inquired of Jokic, who is the man he knew the information came from. General Pandurevic should not be acquitted, Your Honours, for this failure to exercise responsible command. And that concludes my submissions on question 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I waited until the end. Can I just check a judgement reference that Mr. Wood gave at page 14, line 14. It reads as paragraph 2070.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll check that and get back. Turning then to the next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, I would like to be clear about the standard used for superior responsibility. If I'm correct, you referred to reason to know that the soldiers might participate in the killings and then you used the expression "was possible" that they participate in killings. Now, is that the appropriate standard for superior responsibility? In my recollection the Celebici case, which is the leading case on this matter, when it defined superior responsibility referred - as the Trial Chamber correctly says - that the superior knew or had reason to know that a subordinate's criminal act was about to be, was being, or had been realised. There is a slight difference in using the words that an act was about to be committed, it was possible to be committed, because the possibility standard is clearly a threshold which is much, much lower actually. But can you clarify whether your plea remains the same, referring to the appropriate standard?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Trial Chamber was essentially referring -- I think cited specifically to the Strugar appeal judgement in this point, which the Prosecution submits is the proper standard that Your Honours have held is the standard under 7(3). And that is at paragraph 301, and I'll just read that: "Consequently, the Appeals Chamber cannot conclude with certainty that the Trial Chamber properly interpreted the standard of 'had reason to know' as requiring an assessment in the circumstances of the case of whether a superior possessed information that was sufficiently alarming to put him on notice of the risk that crimes might subsequently be carried out by subordinates and justify further inquiry." So this, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits is the proper standard under Article 7(3), as has been articulated by the Appeals Chamber, and as is largely repeated in the Trial Chamber's [Realtime transcript read in error "Prosecution's"] own standard which is put him on notice of possible unlawful acts by his subordinates. Now, the Trial Chamber may have, instead, quoted the language of Strugar specifically, but in the Prosecution's submission it essentially means the same thing and is the correct articulation of the standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification, although I reserve my position on the standard actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. Instead of "2070," it should be "2076," that reference that my colleague pointed out, at page 14, line 14. And I thank him for correcting that. Moving on then, Your Honours, to the third discussion point or question, which is: "Discuss the legal standard applied by the Trial Chamber in finding that Pandurevic did not have reason to know that his -- that crimes 'would be committed with discriminatory intent' as well as the Trial Chamber's factual finding that Pandurevic did not have reason to know that crimes would be committed by Zvornik Brigade members with discriminatory intent." Your Honours, the Trial Chamber erred here in requiring proof that Pandurevic knew the crimes would be committed with discriminatory intent. Under the correct legal standard, the Prosecution must prove that Pandurevic knew or had reason to know that his subordinates might participate in persecutory murder. Though, the Prosecution did not challenge this erroneous legal standard on appeal, we did articulate the correct legal standard in grounds 2(C) and 2(D) of our appeal, at paragraphs 133, 137, and 141. And I'll note also that General Pandurevic articulates a similar legal test at paragraph 236 of his response. This also accords, Your Honours, with the relevant Appeals Chamber jurisprudence in the Strugar appeal judgement at paragraph 302; the Blagojevic and Jokic appeal judgement at paragraph 228 [sic]; and the Krnojelac appeal judgement at paragraphs 52 and 155. In Krnojelac the Appeals Chamber held that aiders and abettors need not share the intent of the perpetrator, but must be aware of the "discriminatory context in which the crime is to be committed." And that is at paragraph 52 of the Krnojelac appeal judgement. So in this case then, Your Honours, the Chamber should have asked itself whether Pandurevic possessed sufficiently alarming information to be put on notice that his subordinates might commit or aid and abet murder and cruel and inhumane treatment with discriminatory intent or with the knowledge of the discriminatory context surrounding these crimes. The only reasonable conclusion on that evidence, Your Honours, is that Pandurevic by noon on the 15th of July, 1995, had, at the very least, reason to know his subordinates might participate in persecutory murder. I've already spelled out in response to the second question the knowledge that Pandurevic had, specifically that he knew a large number would be executed. He -- further, he knew, or it was easy for him to infer, the discriminatory intent of the men he had been told had brought the prisoners to Zvornik -- the Zvornik Brigade area, and that is Beara and Popovic. And that's a finding of the Chamber at 2088. And he also knew of the possibility that his subordinates were participating in this murder. Further, the Chamber found that Pandurevic presided over a brigade in which there existed a "culture of ethnic bias against Muslims," and that's at 2086. This included the commonplace use of ethnic slurs, including documents bearing Pandurevic's own signature. This is a finding at 1398 to 1399 and 2002 of the judgement. And in this respect, I would draw Your Honours' attention in particular to Exhibit P2920. Though the Chamber found that this commonplace use of such language in documents might have been insufficient in itself to prove Pandurevic's genocidal or persecutory intent, it is certainly a reflection of the culture of ethnic bias that reigned in the Zvornik Brigade at the moment that he knew his subordinates might participate in this persecutory murder. The only reasonable conclusion on this evidence, Your Honours, is that Pandurevic at the very least had reason to know that his subordinates might commit or aid and abet murder with persecutory intent or with the knowledge of the discriminatory context surrounding these crimes. Now, this concludes my answer to Your Honours' third question. Unless there are further questions from the Bench, I'm happy to move on to the next question. And that is, for the record: "Discuss the Trial Chamber's finding that it was not possible for Pandurevic to report to the military prosecutor because of the likely interference by the VRS Main Staff in any possible proceedings as well as the Trial Chamber's finding that Pandurevic did take some measures to address the crimes of his subordinates." And this relates primarily to the Prosecution's ground 2(E), Your Honours. And these findings and this holding, the Chamber essentially added an additional element to Article 7(3), by requiring that the Prosecution prove that an accused failed to take all necessary, reasonable, and certain-to-be-effective means to punish his criminal subordinates. Rather than judging General Pandurevic by his own failure to take the necessary and reasonable measures within his means, the Chamber judged Pandurevic by speculating about the possible failures of others in carrying out his criminal referrals, had he made any. And thus, they absolved him of having to take any measures. The law says, Your Honour, that Pandurevic, as commander of criminal subordinates, was required to take the necessary and reasonable steps within his own material ability to initiate and pursue the disciplinary punishment process. And that's from the Kvocka appeal judgement at paragraph 316. It must be shown that he genuinely tried to prevent or punish, and that's from the Halilovic appeal judgement at paragraph 63. He must press the matter, if necessary, to the point of resigning, and that's from the IMTFE judgement at paragraph 448. Further, Your Honours, if a superior's attempts are hampered by somebody else, he is expected to continue his efforts and/or protest against this conduct. And this is from the Strugar trial judgement at paragraph 445. Now, in this case, Your Honours, rather than considering, as it should have, whether Pandurevic could initiate important steps in the disciplinary punishment process by referring his subordinates to the military prosecutor's office, the Chamber instead focused on the potential effectiveness of the military prosecutor's office itself. And in doing so, it erred in law. Now, even, Your Honours, if this were the proper approach, the Chamber's conclusions about the alleged futility of reporting criminal matters to the military prosecutor's office are not supported by the evidence. This evidence showed that a system of military justice, including a Prosecutor's office, had been put in place in 1992 and that it had been taken over in 1993 by the Ministry of Defence. This is at trial judgement footnote 6042, citing the witness Butler at transcript 19607 to 19608. Now, the evidence cited by the Chamber to apparently show that the military prosecutor lacked independence only shows that Gvero helped in setting up the military Prosecutor's office three years earlier, in 1992. This is again at footnote 6042 of the judgement. The only other evidence cited by the Chamber in 6042 refers to military courts, not the prosecutor's office. And even that evidence only shows that Gvero monitored the work of the courts to see how many disciplinary cases were being referred to it. This is data he used to monitor the morale of the units. As Your Honours are aware, morale was part of his competency as the commander. And this is from Milovanovic transcript 12246 to 12247, again cited at paragraph -- or at footnote 6042 of the judgement. So as you can see then, Your Honours, none of this evidence suggests that Gvero in any way interfered with the work of the prosecutor's office. No reasonable finder of fact could have concluded on this evidence that the military prosecutor "was not in fact independent from the Main Staff," as the Chamber did at paragraph 2057. Further, the incident cited -- described in footnote 6043 [Realtime transcript read in error "6042"] of the judgement might show that the MUP failed in its obligations to effectively investigate Srebrenica, but it does not show that the military prosecutor's office failed in any of its obligations, and it says nothing about any interference by the VRS Main Staff. Finally, Your Honours - and this is critically important - there is nothing to suggest that General Pandurevic knew of this alleged lack of independence of the military prosecutor's office. As such, the Chamber should not give him credit for failing to refer criminal matters to an institution for all he knew was competent, professional, and independent. Turning then, Your Honours, to the measures that the Chamber found General Pandurevic actually did take. As the Prosecution points out in ground 2(E), no reasonable finder of fact could have concluded that General Pandurevic had discharged his obligation to punish his criminal subordinates by issuing his self-serving interim combat reports of the 15th of July and of the 18th of July and by having a brief conversation with Krstic on the 27th of July. Rather than being any genuine attempts to punish anybody, these communications were plainly attempts by General Pandurevic to limit his own responsibility for letting the column pass. Now, if you read these carefully, Your Honours, you will see these interim combat reports, they don't mention crimes, they don't mention subordinates, and they weren't addressed to anybody with any official capacity to investigate any crimes. Pandurevic admitted he did not even know whether the allusions he made to crimes could even have been understood by Krstic, the man to whom they were addressed, and that's at trial judgement para 2060. These cannot be said to be a meaningful attempt on the part of Pandurevic to discharge his duty to punish by reporting his subordinates' crimes to an investigative authority. Finally, as to the conversation of the 27th of July, Krstic's response that he would deal with the "problem" did not discharge Pandurevic's own duty to punish, especially where no disciplinary action followed Pandurevic's criminal subordinates. And that concludes my remarks as to this question, Your Honours. I'll continue then to the final question or discussion point number 5, which is: "Discuss whether, in the event that the Appeals Chamber were to grant Pandurevic's argument that he lacked effective control over the Zvornik Brigade in the 4 to 15 July 1995 period, Pandurevic could nonetheless be criminally liable for failing to punish members of the Zvornik Brigade with respect to crimes committed in that time-frame." Let me start first, Your Honours, by reiterating that the Chamber reasonably found that between December 1992 and 3 August 1995, Pandurevic had both de jure command and effective control over the Zvornik Brigade. He's failed to show no reasonable finder of fact could reach this conclusion. Based -- because of this, General Pandurevic's case is in stark contradiction to the leading case on this issue, which is of course the 16 July 2003 decision on interlocutory appeal challenging jurisdiction in relation to command responsibility in the Hadzihasanovic case. That decision, Your Honours, concerned the case of General Hadzihasanovic's co-accused, Colonel Amir Kubura, who had been charged with crimes committed by members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in January 1993, months before he assumed either de jure or de facto command over that unit on the 1st of April of 1993. On these facts, Your Honours, the Chamber [sic] held that: "An accused cannot be charged under Article 7(3) of the Statute for crimes committed by a subordinate before the said accused assumed command over that subordinate." And that's at paragraph 51 of that judgement or that decision. So unlike Kubura, General Pandurevic had assumed the de jure command of the relevant subordinates well before those subordinates committed and aided and abetted murder. As I said, the Chamber found he assumed command in December 1992 and he remained in his post until the 3rd of August, 1995, when he was appointed commander of a brigade tasked with going to the Krajina and his Chief of Staff Obrenovic was officially appointed acting brigade commander. Now, General Pandurevic returned to his post later, but for the purposes of our discussion today, what's important is that no time in between these two critical events his assumption of command in December 1992 and the time he left and Obrenovic took over for him on the 3rd of August, 1995, had Pandurevic ever been relieved of his command. As such, the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision is inapposite. Kubura had neither de jure authority nor effective control and Pandurevic he had both. But, Your Honours, if we must assume the premise of your question, the Prosecution submits that, on the law as it stands, the answer must be no. A superior who has not "assumed command," in the language of Hadzihasanovic, may not be held responsible for the criminal acts that his subordinates committed. However, Your Honours, there are cogent reasons in the interests of justice to depart from the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision. It is contrary to customary international law in that it does violence to the object and purpose of command responsibility, which is, in the words of

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: "... to ensure that there is always someone who will have responsibility for ensuring that the commission of war crimes by a subordinate will not go unpunished ..." This is in the partial dissenting opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen at paragraph 24 of the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision. The Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision is hostile to this end because the it tolerates impunity, Your Honours. Consider the situation in which the subordinates of commander A commit a massacre of 10.000 prisoners at 12.00. At 12.10, before commander A had received sufficiently alarming information about this massacre to even put him on inquiry notice, he is replaced by commander B. Commander B learns of the massacre at 12.20. The soldiers under his command who had executed 10.000 people 20 minutes prior to his assumption of command can now no longer be punished. Under the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision, neither commander has responsibility to punish those subordinates. As Judge Hunt, a Hadzihasanovic dissenter put it, the decision leaves a "gaping hole in the protection which international humanitarian law seeks to provide for the victims of crimes committed contrary to that law." And that's at Judge Hunt's separate and partially dissenting opinion at paragraph 22. This is why, Your Honours, the Prosecution agrees with the 18 ICTY and ICTR Judges, including a majority of Judges on the Oric Appeals Chamber, who have expressed views contrary to the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision. It should be overturned, for the reasons stated with far greater eloquence than I can muster by Judges Shahabuddeen, Hunt, Liu, and Schomburg in their declarations and dissenting opinions in Hadzihasanovic and in Oric. In addition to being wrong in law and unpopular among Judges, the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility decision is also contrary to common sense, as its application to these facts would illustrate. General Pandurevic is a commander who was unquestionably in formal command of his brigade during his brief 11-day absence from his desk at the Standard Barracks. He is a commander who is leading members of that same brigade in combat a mere 40 kilometres from his barracks, but still within the same corps, still within the same army. He's a commander who learned immediately upon his return to his barracks that his subordinates were committing criminal acts, and he's a commander who then learned that his subordinates had been participating in the murder operation since just two days before his return. It defies logic and common sense, Your Honours, in these circumstances to find that this commander has no obligation whatever to punish those troops. And that concludes my remarks about this final discussion point, Your Honours. Unless there are further questions, I'll -- Your Honour, in response to General -- or to Your Honour, Judge Pocar's question, I have a further cite. The Nahimana appeal judgement at paragraph 791: "The reason to know standard is met when the superior had some general information in his possession which would put him on notice of possible unlawful acts by his subordinates." And this is further support for the Prosecution's argument that this is the correct legal standard. And again, unless there's any questions at this moment I can turn the podium over to my colleague, Mr. Kremer, unless Your Honours would prefer to take a break at this time. I'm in your hands.

utterances.text: Your Honours, before I start my submissions, I would like to deal with a few housekeeping matters relating to the transcript following Mr. Wood's submissions. Line 5, page 13, the transcript says "triggered until he found out completely that his subordinates had" and Mr. Wood said "triggered until he had found out concretely that the subordinates had." The next one is page 17, line 12, Mr. Wood said, "Trial Chamber's own standard," but it was reported in the transcript as "Prosecution's own standard." Obviously that's not correct. utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Now, moving to the Prosecution's submission on ground 1, subgrounds 1(A) and 1(B), I'll start by saying that the essence of the Prosecution appeal is that the Chamber erred by acquitting Vinko Pandurevic for the mass killings committed in the Zvornik area from noon on 15 July onwards. He was convicted in part for these killings, but the Chamber's findings as to the level of his responsibility do not reflect the reality of the situation. Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law and/or in fact when it failed to find that Pandurevic became a member of the joint criminal enterprise to murder or, alternatively, became an -- or was an aider and abettor in the extermination, murder, and persecutions committed in the Zvornik area with the participation of his subordinates after he returned to the Zvornik Brigade on 15 July. There is a basic flaw in the judgement. The Trial Chamber offered only cursory and erroneous reasons for its conclusions on the elements of contribution and shared intent for Pandurevic's joint criminal enterprise liability. For aiding and abetting of murder, extermination, and persecutions within the murder operation, the Chamber failed to discuss or adjudicate Pandurevic's criminal responsibility at all. But apart from these legal errors, the Chamber erred as a matter of fact. As we explain in our brief, there was overwhelming evidence of Pandurevic's involvement and support of the murder operation both through the exercise of command and control of his troops taking part in the murder operation and his failures to meet his legal duties to protect the Bosnian Muslim prisoners who were murdered in his zone of responsibility. The Trial Chamber's detailed factual findings of Pandurevic's knowledge and his acts and omissions, his contributions, should have led the Trial Chamber to conclude that Pandurevic shared the intent and was a member of the joint criminal enterprise to murder or, at the very least, an aider and abettor of the crimes of the murder operation. Now, how did the Trial Chamber err? Simply, it disregarded relevant evidence and in fact its own factual findings. As a result, the Chamber made inconsistent and contradictory findings on Pandurevic's knowledge, leading to the challenged findings on contributions and shared intent. The Trial Chamber found that on 15 July Pandurevic knew of the plan to murder the able-bodied Bosnian Muslim males from Srebrenica and his subordinates' participation in this murder operation. Specifically, it found that on 15 July at noon Pandurevic learned of the key features of the murder plan and the Zvornik Brigade's involvement in its execution. I'll now turn to my first slide. Your Honours can see the Chamber's relevant language at paragraph 1861 of the judgement. In the highlighted portion it says clearly that -- is it up? "Obrenovic informed Pandurevic that pursuant to Mladic's order, Beara and Popovic had brought a large number of prisoners from Bratunac to the Zvornik sector, where they were executing them and that, according to Jokic, there were enormous problems with the guarding, execution, and burial of prisoners. Pandurevic then asked why the civilian protection was not performing the burials." And although that last sentence may not seem connected, I'll explain why it's very important in a moment. Some hundred paragraphs later, the Chamber confirmed the finding of Pandurevic's knowledge at paragraphs 1959 and 1960 and referred back in its footnote to paragraph 1861. You can see this in the next slide. I refer you to, first of all, paragraph 1959, where the Chamber concluded that it: "... is ultimately satisfied beyond all reasonable doubt that on 15 July Pandurevic was told by Obrenovic about the detention, execution, and burial of the prisoners in the Zvornik area as described by PW-168." It goes on at paragraph 1960, and I've highlighted the relevant passage, that the Chamber concluded that: "... Pandurevic thus knew that pursuant to Mladic's order, Beara and Popovic had brought a large number of prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik where they were being executed, and that according to Jokic, there were enormous problems with the guarding, execution, and burial of these prisoners. In light of this knowledge on the part of Pandurevic, the Trial Chamber therefore finds that at this point on 15 July" and I emphasise this "he knew of the plan to murder the able-bodied Bosnian Muslim males from Srebrenica." Importantly, these passages show that the Trial Chamber rejected Pandurevic's denial that he and Obrenovic had had this conversation, just as it rejected most of Pandurevic's denials or innocent explanations of incriminating evidence against him. It found that Pandurevic knew that the murder operation was in full swing on July 15, noon. The Chamber also found that Pandurevic knew that the murder operation was impacting his decision-making through his own words dictated a few hours later in his 15 July interim combat report. At paragraph 4 of this report, which is replicated in paragraph 1870 of the judgement, Pandurevic reported: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of this terrain." I'll now turn to our third slide. As highlighted in the slide before you, in paragraph 1948 the Chamber found that: "... the first part of the sentence of paragraph 4 of" his 15 July report which I just read to you, "Pandurevic is cryptically referring to the additional burden for the brigade of guarding prisoners as well as the security concerns caused by the presence of the prisoners in Zvornik." The Trial Chamber further found that: "... the second part," and I'm quoting here, "of the sentence of that paragraph, Pandurevic is referring to the burden to the brigade of assisting with the burial of the prisoners who had been brought by others to the Zvornik area for execution." And finally, the Trial Chamber concluded that the report itself was: "... strong evidence that on 15 July, Pandurevic was aware not only of prisoners but also of executions in the Zvornik area." Your Honours, these findings are significant, as together they clearly show the Chamber was satisfied that by the 15th of July Pandurevic knew of the murder operation and that his Zvornik Brigade resources were tied up in it. However, when the time came to assess his contributions and shared intent, the Trial Chamber then inexplicably ignored these findings. I'll now take you to the fourth slide, which shows the relevant portion of paragraph 1972, where it does, as I've just stated. As reflected in the highlighted passage, the Chamber found that: "... having considered the precise information provided by Obrenovic on 15 July, the Trial Chamber is not convinced that it is sufficient in itself or in combination with the information provided by Grujic, to find that at this point Pandurevic knew that members of the Zvornik Brigade were committing or aiding and abetting crimes. Notably, he was neither told nor did he seek any specifics as to the involvement of the Zvornik Brigade in the murder operation, brigade members' knowledge of the executions, or the particular responsibilities of his chief of security in the operation. While undoubtedly the information triggered his obligations under superior responsibility as will be discussed later, for the purposes of assessing his participation in the crimes and contributions to the JCE, the Trial Chamber is not satisfied that the knowledge requirement for commission by omission has been met." And we have a ground of appeal that deals with the error of applying commission by omission standard for assessing acts and contributions or acts and omissions as contributions to the JCE. The Chamber contradicts itself by finding that Pandurevic did not know that members of the Zvornik Brigade were involved in the crimes at this stage. The missing link of knowledge on the 15th at noon is precisely what the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 1948 that Pandurevic's 15 July report established. And if I can just repeat the relevant portion of paragraph 1948: "The Trial Chamber finds that in the first part of the sentence of paragraph 4 of the 15 July interim combat report, Pandurevic is cryptically referring to the additional burden for the brigade of guarding prisoners as well as security concerns caused by the presence of those prisoners in Zvornik. The Trial Chamber further finds that in the second part of sentence of that paragraph, Pandurevic is referring to the burden of the brigade of assisting with the burial of the prisoners who had been brought by others to the Zvornik Brigade for execution. Paragraph 1948 makes clear that by the 15 of July, Pandurevic did know that the Zvornik Brigade, his men and his assets, were involved in the murder operation. A closer examination of paragraph 1972 reveals the error and how it came to be. That error is that the Trial Chamber limited its assessment of Pandurevic's knowledge of the Zvornik Brigade's involvement in the murder operation to what he learned in the conversations with Obrenovic and Grujic on 15 July. Paragraph 1972 tellingly ignores: One, the information Pandurevic himself revealed about the state of his knowledge of the murder operation in the 15 July report; and two, the contextual facts as to the involvement of the Zvornik Brigade resources in the murder operation, which would have informed Pandurevic as Zvornik Brigade commander on his return. With this additional information, a very different picture emerges than the one the Trial Chamber described in making its findings at paragraphs 1972 and 1973. At noon on 15 July, Pandurevic knew that Jokic had informed Obrenovic that he, Jokic, "had enormous problems with the security and burial of prisoners." Because Jokic had enormous problems with security and burial, Pandurevic knew that Jokic and other Zvornik Brigade members were participating in security, guarding, and burial activities for the murder operation. The context of information he received shows that Jokic did not have enormous problems alone. The evidence shows that the security of prisoners was a responsibility customarily falling to the brigade military police. Burials required the involvement of members of and equipment from the engineering company. And I refer Your Honours to judgement paragraphs 1935, 2038, and transcript pages 15886, 16228 to 16229. Pandurevic's response to Obrenovic's -- I'm sorry, to Obrenovic on Jokic's report - "Why the civilian protection were not performing the burials" from 1861 reflected also in trial judgement paragraph 1939 [sic] - demonstrated that he understood at the very least that Jokic and the Zvornik Brigade engineering company were involved in burying the prisoners. Your Honours will recall that Beara had approached the civilian authorities in both Bratunac and Zvornik to assist in the burial of executed prisoners. You will find that at trial judgement paragraphs 1263 to 1271 for Bratunac and paragraph 1278 [Realtime transcript read in error "1287"] for Zvornik. Obrenovic's account of the problems facing the Zvornik Brigade in the murder operation included the guarding and the executions. And that's paragraph 1861, 1935 and 1948. You're familiar with two of those three references. From this conversation, Pandurevic knew that members of the Zvornik Brigade were actively involved in the murder operation and its crimes. This alone contradicts the Chamber's findings at paragraph 1972 that Pandurevic did not have sufficient information concerning the involvement of the Zvornik Brigade in the murder operation. But the Trial Chamber doesn't stop there. The Trial Chamber makes an additional finding at 1973 that Pandurevic's knowledge of the members of the Zvornik Brigade had participated in guarding prisoners who had been detained in the Zvornik area and had participated in the burials of the executed prisoners was not acquired until the evening of 16 July after the murder operation was nearly complete is equally wrong, for the same reason and the same factual basis and the same factual findings that the Trial Chamber had made earlier in its judgement which I've referred to. While Pandurevic may have learned more details over the following days about the Zvornik Brigade members involved, the exact numbers and locations of detention, murder, and burial sites, these specifics were not necessary given his information and his knowledge on 15 July that systematic murders and exterminations were underway at various sites across his sector. No reasonable Trial Chamber could have found otherwise. The Trial Chamber's erroneous conclusion is further reflected in light of the Zvornik Brigade and Zvornik Brigade command's extensive involvement in the implementation of the murder operation on 15 and 16 July, when Pandurevic was back in Zvornik and during which up to 3.000 Bosnian Muslim prisoners were executed and buried in his zone of responsibility. Now I'll move to the next slide. Your Honours will see on your screen Exhibit P1876 depicting the Zvornik Brigade zone of responsibility which we've titled July 14, the day before Pandurevic returned to Standard Barracks. We have added information to this map to show how the various Zvornik Brigade assets and personnel were used in the murder operation on that day. At the left of the map, you will see the seven battalion zones of the Zvornik Brigade, left-middle of the map, indicated by numbers and divided by the pink lines. At the bottom right of the map, you can see Karakaj, which is where the Zvornik Brigade was based at the Standard Barracks. The small red arrows that you can see at the bottom of the map represent the approaching column of Bosnian Muslims. And the arrows are heading in the direction of the 7.pb and 4.pb on the bottom left-hand side. The red rectangles that you see represent schools that served as places of detention for prisoners before their executions. The red circles represent execution sites. As you can see at the top left, the different-coloured arrows represent the movements of different types of Zvornik Brigade resources: Green for military, blue for military security or military police, orange for engineering assets, and purple for logistics assets. The arrows are accompanied by reference to the source of information that -- about that moment -- or about that movement, I'm sorry. I will note that the arrows do not represent the exact path which the Zvornik Brigade resources or personnel were sent, but do reflect from which brigades or areas the Zvornik Brigade resources and personnel were sent to the relevant site. Looking at this map, and you will see two more maps for each of the days, the 15th and the 16th of July, first starting with the 14th of July map. This map illustrates three important points: First, as you can see on 14 July, the Zvornik Brigade was actively rendering aid to the ongoing murder operation with many resources converging on the Grbavci school and Orahovac, where the first mass execution of the murder operation was occurring in the Zvornik area. And the trial references are there, trial judgement 471 to 489. Second, the deployment of Zvornik Brigade resources to these sites was not spontaneous or arbitrary. Orders were issued by senior staff members of the Zvornik Brigade, including Obrenovic, Pandurevic's Chief of Staff; and Jasikovac, Pandurevic's commander of the Zvornik Brigade military police; and Ristic, the acting commander of the 4th Battalion. Trial judgement paragraphs 471, 478 to 486, and 1879. And the third point is that assets from the 4th Battalion were engaged in the murder operation as the column was nearing the 4th Battalion's area of responsibility. This fact will become more relevant in a moment. And I refer you to trial judgement 479 to 486. And so let's just move on to the slide depicting the activities of the 15th of July. Again, this map displays the distribution of Zvornik Brigade assets and personnel to the various sites relevant to the murder operation. As Your Honours know and have heard all week, it is on this day that Pandurevic is sent back to Zvornik with orders from Krstic to crush the column. The column is depicted on this map at the rear areas of the 4th, 6th, and 7th Battalions. Upon receiving Krstic's orders, Pandurevic made two phone calls to the Zvornik Brigade at 8.55 and at 9.10 in the morning. And I refer you to transcript -- or to judgement paragraph 1860 and Exhibits P1172c and P1174c. I point out that during those calls, Pandurevic demanded reports on the combat situation and focused in particular on the areas of the 4th, 6th, and 7th Battalions. As you can see on the map, on the 15th of July, the 6th Battalion, including the 6th Battalion commander Stanisic, was immersed in the murder operation. In particular, Stanisic ordered trucks and drivers to the Petkovci school to move prisoners to the nearby execution site at the dam and then, after the shootings, to move more than 800 bodies to the mass grave. That's found at trial judgement paragraphs 499 to 501. I point out at this point that apart from the resources of the 4th and 6th Battalions, other battalions of the Zvornik Brigade were engaged in the murder operation. On 15 July, as reflected in this map, in the north of the Zvornik Brigade -- of responsibility, Zvornik Brigade assets and personnel were used at the Rocevic school and the Kozluk gravel pit, including soldiers in the execution of prisoners and MP in the guarding of prisoners. 1st [Realtime transcript read in error "11"] Battalion soldiers were dispatched to the Kula school to relieve those who had been guarding prisoners there since the 14th. Further, engineering resources were still engaged at Orahovac. And I refer you to trial judgement paragraphs 490, 501, 507 to 511, 515, 518 to 520, 530 to 531. Senior members of the Zvornik Brigade were also involved in these crimes, including 2nd Battalion Commander Acimovic, Zvornik Brigade MP commander Jasikovac, and Zvornik Brigade duty officer and chief of engineering Jokic, all issued orders tasking their men with guarding, executing, and burial duties at Orahovac, Rocevic school, and Kozluk. And I refer you to paragraphs 489 to 490, 507 to 511, 515, 517 to 522. This slide and my remarks demonstrate two things: First, the extent of the Zvornik Brigade's involvement in all aspects of the killing operation, both in terms of members and resources and senior commanders from the Zvornik Brigade. The detentions, killings, and burials of several thousand Bosnian Muslim prisoners could not have occurred without the extensive participation of the Zvornik Brigade; second, it shows that the mass killings were ongoing after Pandurevic returned at noon on 15 July. The killings at Petkovci dam and Kozluk gravel pit were among the biggest killings in the murder operation. The first piece of information Pandurevic received from his Chief of Staff, Obrenovic, was that his troops were involved in the mass killings on Mladic's orders and yet he decided to let them continue. It is against this backdrop of his subordinates' involvement in the murder operation - with the Zvornik Brigade's resources stretched thin due to the demands of the ongoing murder operation - that Pandurevic drafted his 7.25 interim combat report. And I refer you to paragraph 1868. This report is critical to the entire factual analysis that I am doing now to show how wrong the Chamber -- Trial Chamber was in paragraphs 1972 and 1973 in assessing his knowledge for the purpose of looking at his contributions and the assessment of shared intent. Pandurevic's 15 July report, which is found in full in Exhibit P329, confirms his command decision to endorse the murder operation by having permitted his brigade's continued participation in it. After Pandurevic reports "all brigade forces are fully engaged and we have no reserves," he reports on the murder operation. By reporting "all forces are engaged," Pandurevic is telling his superiors that he knows that his subordinates from the 4th and 6th Battalions together with his military police and engineering company are participating in the murder operation in Orahovac, Kozluk, and Petkovci. Pandurevic reports that material and other resource limitations impact on his ability to continue to "take care of these problems," which the Chamber found included the Zvornik Brigade's involvement in the murder operation. Pandurevic's command authority to deal with these problems was made very clear by his threat to let the column go. And that's found at paragraphs 1962 to 1963. But Pandurevic made no threat to let the prisoners go. As events unfolded during the 15th and all day on the 16th, his subordinates continued to guards and transport Bosnian Muslim prisoners, supply fuel and ammunition to detention and execution sites, transport and/or bury executed prisoners in unmarked mass graves, and, at least in one case, execute prisoners. And that leads me to the final slide of July 16th, again showing the distribution of Zvornik Brigade assets and personnel to the relevant sites. By 16 July, the column was fighting the Zvornik Brigade in the area near Baljkovica, near the 4th and 6th Battalions' zones. Pandurevic's 15 July report showed that the Zvornik Brigade was desperate for resources and was calling for reinforcements. But at the same time, orders from the Zvornik Brigade commanders dispatched resources away from the front lines, continuing to dedicate them to the murder operation. Zvornik Brigade 6th Battalion soldiers travelled away from the front lines to Petkovci school to assist in moving bodies to the Petkovci dam, paragraph 1881. The commander of the 1st Battalion work platoon, Lakic, ordered men to the Kula school to stand guard while prisoners were put on buses that brought them to the Zvornik Brigade's military farm near Branjevo for execution by the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and that's at paragraphs 533 to 535, 537 to 542. Lakic then ordered his men to the Pilica cultural centre, where soldiers from Bratunac had executed another 500 prisoners. Lakic's men loaded the bodies into trucks and transported them to the Branjevo Military Farm for burial. Burials at Branjevo had to continue into the next day, trial judgement paragraphs 542 to 546. Zvornik Brigade engineering chief Jokic ordered his 2nd Platoon to Kozluk to continue burying those who had been executed the day before. An excavator was also dispatched. That's at paragraph 521 to 522 and Exhibit P301. Zvornik Brigade engineering personnel were also at Orahovac that day. A truck repeatedly travelled between two mass grave-sites, and that's found at Exhibits P297 and P298. And finally, the map reflects the Zvornik Brigade military police spent all day 16 July at three key murder operation sites in Pilica, Rocevic, and Kula, and that's Exhibit P296. It is in this setting that Pandurevic realised that he could not fight the column and the 2nd ABiH Corps -- the 2nd Corps of the ABiH and that his men and the town of Zvornik were at risk. So he decided to negotiate a resolution to allow the column to pass through Zvornik Brigade territory into ABiH territory. His offer to allow the civilians to pass and the military component to surrender was rejected. The fighting continued. Finally, an agreement to let the entire column through Zvornik Brigade lines was implemented between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m. The agreement included a cease-fire. Why, you say or you ask yourself, is a cease-fire relevant? Because it would have allowed Pandurevic time to focus on his other immediate problem, specifically the murder operation, the only other burden on his men and materials at the time. And what happened? When the corridor was opened on the afternoon of 16 July and the column was allowed to pass, hundreds of Muslim prisoners were being murdered at the Branjevo Farm and 500 Muslims waited for execution at the Pilica cultural centre later that day. Significant amounts of men and materials of the Zvornik Brigade were involved in conducting these executions, as well as the continuing burial operations at Orahovac, Petkovci, and Kozluk. I refer you to paragraphs 521 to 522, 532 to 547, 1881, Exhibits P297, P298, and P301. Like his 15 July interim combat report, Pandurevic's 16 July interim combat report, found at Exhibit 7DP330, confirmed his command decisions. He reported on the attacks by the 2nd Corps and the attacks from the column. He also reported on his decision to let the column through. While he does not report on his third problem, his brigade's burden caused by the murder operation which continued without incident with the support of the Zvornik Brigade resources, Pandurevic's command decisions ensured the successful completion of the murder operation. The cease-fire to let the column pass eliminated the risk that Zvornik Brigade resources [sic] engaged in the murder operation might be needed to fight the column at the front line. As I have already mentioned, Pandurevic was not afraid to disobey superior orders. By letting the column pass through Zvornik Brigade lines to Bosnian Muslim territory, Pandurevic chose the safety of his men and the protection of the VRS positions along the combat lines over his clear superior orders to crush and destroy the column. Similarly, the option to protect the prisoners being murdered in the Zvornik zone of responsibility was within Pandurevic's material ability. And I refer you to a more fulsome discussion in our appeal brief at paragraph 77 to 82. In this full context, Pandurevic's knowledge and contributions are clear and demonstrate beyond any reasonable doubt that he shared the intent of the JCE to murder. Once he learned of Mladic's manifestly illegal order to carry out the murder operation in his zone of responsibility, Pandurevic, as a commander, had a choice. He could choose to accept the order and command the fulfilment of the murder operation tasks assigned to his brigade, which he did, or he could refuse the order, rescind Obrenovic's initial command, and cease his brigade's involvement in the murder operation. Because Pandurevic chose to adopt Mladic's manifestly illegal order, he must accept responsibility for that decision. And as I have said in my submissions and I hope convinced you from the discussion of the facts, if the Chamber had looked at the interim combat reports and the facts on the ground and the participation of his brigades in the murder operation in light of those reports, the only conclusion you can come to on his knowledge and his contributions is together they equalled his shared -- or proved and established his shared intent. Although the plan to murder the Bosnian Muslim prisoners did not originate from Pandurevic, his endorsement and participation ensured the operation's success. In conclusion, the only reasonable conclusion is that Pandurevic decided that the murder operation tasks should be carried out. Pandurevic's intent meets the JCE threshold. In respect of the Prosecution's alternative ground of aiding and abetting, our position is that the only reasonable conclusion open to the Trial Chamber, had it done the proper analysis and made the required findings, was that Pandurevic knew that the Bosnian Muslim prisoners were brought to the Zvornik zone of responsibility to be executed and that by allowing his brigade to continue to participate in the murder operation by guarding, burying, and providing logistical support to the executors or to the people committing the killings, he would assist in murder, extermination, and persecutions. I refer to the Krstic appeal judgement which succinctly describes the situation that we find ourselves in here at paragraph 137: "Radislav Krstic was aware that the Main Staff had insufficient resources of its own to carry out the executions and that, without the use of Drina ... resources, the Main Staff would not be able to implement its genocidal plan. Krstic knew that by allowing Drina Corps resources to be used he was making a substantial contribution to the execution of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners. Although the evidence suggests that Radislav Krstic was not a supporter of the plan, as Commander of the Drina Corps he permitted the Main Staff to call upon Drina Corps resources and to employ those resources. The criminal liability of Krstic is therefore more properly expressed as that of an aider and abettor ..." But we're talking here about Krstic in the context of aiding and abetting genocide or committing genocide, a discussion that is different slightly for Pandurevic because Pandurevic was found not to have genocidal intent and that has not been appealed. But the same analysis and conclusion can apply in the alternative to Pandurevic, but our primary position is, and based on my submissions or our submissions, is that Pandurevic's intent was shared with the other JCE members, and that is to fully support and assist through his orders the murder operation in full knowledge of it and all of his contributions substantially contributed to -- or significantly contributed to it in the JCE context and substantially contributed to it in the aiding and abetting context. I'm not sure if I need get into this, it's been covered in earlier submissions by my colleague, Mr. Milaninia, and that is the specific direction issue. If Your Honours choose to go there and the Perisic point, simply the Prosecution submits that the culpable link connecting General Pandurevic to the crimes is evident from his subordinates' participation in the murder operation, his knowledge of it, and the fact that their contribution - as is evidenced by the paragraphs referred to connected with the charts that I've shown - demonstrate that the contribution was substantial. Pandurevic was present in the zone of responsibility when the crimes were being committed, he had knowledge of them and his subordinates' involvement. His command and control over the troops, as demonstrated by his actions, orders, and reporting show and make the culpable link. And ultimately the fact that his -- and as we can see the proximity to the crimes and the locations of -- to all of the crimes, whether it be execution sites, detention centre, also confirms the links. Those are my submissions on why the Trial Chamber erred, both in law and in fact, in acquitting General Pandurevic of being a member of the joint criminal enterprise to murder or, in the alternative -- and also acquitting him in the alternative of aiding and abetting murder, extermination, and persecutions. Subject to any questions which you may have, those are my submissions. And depending on if there's any time remaining, I would pass on to Mr. Wood for short comments on sentencing. But before I do -- before I -- perhaps before Your Honour answers that question, a couple of housekeeping issues. At line 14, page 36, "1287" should be "1278." And at line 3 on page 40, it says "11 Battalion" and that should read "1st Battalion," so obviously a typographical mistake. But as to time, I'm in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Finally then, Your Honours, a few words about sentencing. General Pandurevic bears responsibility for the forcible transfer of tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims, men, women, and children, and the murders of up to 2500 Bosnian Muslim men and boys. Those killed included boys as young as 14 and men as old as 84. General Pandurevic also allowed ten wounded soldiers to be handed over to a man he knew would execute them. His crimes continued to resonate in the Bosnian Muslim community 18 years on, even as he looks forward to the application for early release that his counsel has told you will follow these proceedings. He failed at every decisive moment to do what the international community demanded of him, to protect prisoners even though all that was required of him was to issue a simple order. By any measure, Your Honours, in any courtroom, in any country anywhere in the world, these crimes would be considered to be so grave as to merit a sentence far greater than 13 years. It's a sentence that's so manifestly inadequate that it shows the Chamber failed to exercise its discretion properly. First, the sentence fails to take into account the inherent gravity of General Pandurevic's failure as a commander to prevent breaches of international humanitarian law. Rather than act to protect the prisoners, Your Honours, he presided over a brigade with a culture of ethnic bias against Bosnian Muslims, a brigade that took part in unspeakable episodes of murder and cruel treatment. Second, as we've argued, his sentence bears no relation whatsoever to the likely sentences of his subordinates for the roles they played in the murders and forcible transfers. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the maximum sentence for the gravest crimes is 45 years. In comparison, his 13-year sentence is a trifle. Finally, Your Honours, the Chamber erred in granting any mitigation for his role in letting the column pass through his lines. Remember, Your Honours, the people in this column were people that he himself had forcibly expelled from Srebrenica in the previous days and they were people that he did his level best to murder in the 24 hours following his return to the Zvornik Brigade. He put these people in grave danger, he worked hard to kill them, but he simply couldn't. A hostage taker shouldn't get credit for freeing hostages who had already escaped his clutches despite his best efforts to kill them. His act of letting the column pass cannot be understood as any kind of humanitarian gesture. Rather, it was an expression of his failure as a commander to do as he was told, which is to crush and to kill the column. For these reasons, Pandurevic's crimes demand a sentence at the highest end of the sentencing spectrum. His 13-year sentence is an affront to the victims in this case and it fails to adequately express the outrage of the international community. The Prosecution asks you to revise this sentence and impose a penalty commensurate with the gravity of Pandurevic's crimes and his conduct. And that concludes our brief remarks on sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel for Mr. Popovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, the Defence of Popovic maintains that Mr. Popovic is neither guilty of genocide nor of conspiracy to commit genocide. These arguments are set out in our response to the Prosecution's appeal brief paragraphs 2 to 8 and in our appeal in paragraphs 17 through 27, 30 through 35, 41, 49, 54, 65, 67, 863 [sic], 171 through 178, 191, 195, 238 through 239, 255, 330 -- 303, excuse me, 349, and 402 and in the six grounds of our notice of appeal, paragraphs 394 through 397. Then it not be repeated at length here. I will repeat, however, that the Trial Chamber construed every piece of evidence in the way the most harmful for Popovic, including finding him guilty for conspiracy to commit genocide. Indeed, reference to fairness in this context is almost cynical. I will not repeat our arguments from the response brief -- from our response brief, but I'd just like to comment yesterday's reference by the Prosecution to Gatete appeal judgement as to cumulative convictions but for genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide.
