We submit that such conviction from the Appeals Chamber would violate the right on the appeal provided in the Article 24(2) of the Statute. Precisely, Mr. Popovic, in case of conviction, would be deprived of his right to appeal, and on this point we refer to the dissenting opinion of Judge Pocar in Gatete appeal judgement. It is in chapter 7-2. I will just quote this part, where it's stated: "The absence of any right whatever to appeal such a conviction say in the case where the matter is remitted to the Trial Chamber is likely to infringe upon the fundamental principle of fairness recognised both in international law and many national legal systems." In this context we believe that such a conviction would violate the principle -- the elementary principle of fairness too. It concludes my submission, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel for Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and may it please the Judges of this Chamber. The actus reus of conspiracy to commit genocide is the act of entering into an agreement to commit genocide. There was no evidence adduced at trial that Mr. Beara entered into any such agreement. The Prosecution did not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Beara was present at any meetings at which the Trial Chamber determined the plan was formulated. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Beara's conduct - and that's in paragraph 1318 of the Trial Chamber's judgement - demonstrated that he had genocidal intent. We have already argued that Mr. Beara did not possess genocidal intent, given his acquittal of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly deport the women and children from Srebrenica. This showed, again, as we previously argued, that Mr. Beara did not have the genocidal intent to destroy that part of the group consisting of the Bosnian Muslims of Eastern Bosnia. While the Trial Chamber did acquit Mr. Beara of the forcible transfer charge, we note further the Trial Chamber's finding that Mr. Beara knew of the forcible transfer but did not make any significant contribution toward the forcible transfer operation. We note for the sake of accuracy and for the relevancy, if any, when considered with the conspiracy charge, that even the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Mr. Beara knew of the forcible - and I'm underlining the word "forcible" - even the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Mr. Beara knew of the forcible transfer is open to serious doubt. There was only one piece of evidence in the case that showed any knowledge of Mr. Beara of the transfer of the women and children, and that consisted of the testimony of the witness Celanovic, the desk officer of the Bratunac Brigade. Celanovic testified that on the evening of July 13th he was meeting with Mr. Beara and he told Mr. Beara that he, Celanovic, had security concerns about the number of prisoners in the area. And he was asking Beara when they could be transported out of the Bratunac area. According to Celanovic's testimony - and that's on pages 6640-6641 of the trial transcript - Mr. Beara stated that they would have to wait until the other vehicles that had transported the women and children had returned. And that's in the Trial Chamber's judgement at paragraph 1307. Celanovic's testimony does show that Mr. Beara had some knowledge of the fact that women and children were being bussed from Srebrenica, but where is the evidence that Mr. Beara knew that this was a forcible transfer operation? We say there was no such evidence. It is Directive 7 and following directives to that that are usually cited by the Prosecution to show the knowledge of the Main Staff, of which Mr. Beara was a member of course, that the expulsion of Bosnian Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave was the ultimate goal. But as stated by the Appeals Chamber in the Krstic case at paragraph 90, and I quote: "Directives 7 and 7.1 are insufficiently clear to establish that there was a genocidal intent on the part of the members of the Main Staff who issued them. Indeed, the Trial Chamber did not even find that those who issued Directives 7 and 7.1 had genocidal intent. Concluding, instead, that the genocidal plan crystallised at a later stage." As in the Krstic case, the directives and the meetings leading up to the July 13/14 time-period, at which Mr. Beara was not present, are the only evidence that the Prosecution offered of an alleged conspiracy to commit genocide in Mr. Beara's case. However, the Trial Chamber did not even refer to any such evidence, concluding that Mr. Beara was guilty of conspiracy, and that's paragraph 1322 of the judgement. Instead, the Trial Chamber stated very generally, and I quote: "Conspiracy to commit genocide can be inferred from co-ordinated actions by individuals who have a common purpose and are acting within a unified framework. Evidence has already been examined of the co-ordinated actions and unifying framework of those who participated in the operation to murder the able-bodied Bosnian Muslim males from Srebrenica in July 1995, including Beara." And at this point the Trial Chamber refers to footnote 4316, which cite passages relating only to the joint criminal enterprise to murder. Continuing with my quotation from the Trial Chamber: "Based upon this evidence, the Trial Chamber concludes that Beara entered into an agreement to commit genocide and he himself possessed specific intent to commit genocide." As with its conviction of Mr. Beara of genocide, the Trial Chamber based its finding of conspiracy to commit genocide solely on Mr. Beara's participation in the joint criminal enterprise to murder. Our argument is similar regarding genocidal intent here on the conspiracy conviction to our argument on the genocide conviction. The evidence that Mr. Beara participated in the murder operation is not enough to show that he's guilty of the act of entering into an agreement to commit genocide, especially in light of his lack of genocidal intent via his acquittal on the forcible transfer charge. If Mr. Beara did not have genocidal intent, he did not commit genocide. If he did not commit genocide, the Trial Chamber cannot reasonably conclude that the alleged genocidal act, which is murder only in Mr. Beara's case, demonstrated conspiracy to commit genocide. Inferring conspiracy from acts of murder - awful as that is - but inferring conspiracy from acts of murder is not the only reasonable inference to be drawn, especially given the absence of any direct evidence of any act by Mr. Beara constituting entering into an agreement to commit genocide. And that, Your Honours, is our presentation. I'd be happy to answer any questions if you have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have no questions. I understand counsel for Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be extremely brief. If we consider the submissions of the Prosecution from a purely legal standpoint without referring to the facts, the Prosecution is absolutely right; however, the logic of the Prosecution is reversed because the Trial Chamber did not commit an error by acquitting Miletic for Count 5 but by convicting him for -- on Count 4, that's the basis of our arguments on the factual basis that our arguments rest for acquittal on charge 4. I refer to the submissions I set out yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take the break now and, evidently, we can't break for an hour as I suggested, we must break for one and a half hours. So we should be back at five minutes to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, honourable Judges. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. I'd like to apologise in advance, I do not see one of the members of the Bench and I apologise for this. Mr. President, I will have the pleasure this afternoon of responding to the Prosecution appeal on behalf of Mr. Nikolic. In doing so, I will respond to both questions put to the parties in the Appeals Chamber's order dated 6 November 2013. The Prosecution advances two grounds of appeal, namely, ground 7, that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Drago Nikolic did not have genocidal intent; and also ground 8, that the 35-years' imprisonment sentence imposed on Drago Nikolic is inadequate and too low. With respect to this second ground, ground number 8 on sentence, I believe, Mr. President, that we have made our position very clear throughout this appeal, that we believe the sentence to be excessive. That was in our appeal brief from paragraphs 5 to 45 in -- concerning the Prosecution appeal, we rely on our argument which can be found in our response at paragraphs 191 to 259. Of course, Mr. President, you will not be surprised to hear that it is our position that both Prosecution grounds should be dismissed in their entirety. Before I begin, however, I wish to bring two preliminary matters, and the first one has to do with something found in the Prosecution response at paragraphs 254, which I would like to draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to. In its brief and reply and again this morning, Mr. President, arguing ground 7, the Prosecution returns to the issue of the actions which would have been taken by Drago Nikolic which he would have pursued in the persistent and determined manner. I refer here to paragraphs 247 to 262. Now, in this regard paragraphs 254 reads as follows: "During the morning of 14 July, Nikolic called Slavko Peric, assistant commander for intelligence and security, of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. Nikolic repeated the contents of a coded telegram sent earlier by the Zvornik Brigade command." The words I wish to draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber on are simply those words "coded telegram." The reason being is that in this paragraph the Prosecution refers to paragraphs 1359 and 1360 of the judgement, where there is absolutely no mention of a coded telegram. Is this an oversight? We don't believe so, Mr. President. What is important, however, is that the only person who has mentioned a coded telegram in this case or the use of a coded telegram is the commander of the 2nd Battalion, Acimovic. And of course you've heard our argument previously that we say that he advanced the argument of coded telegrams to shield his responsibility and that the Trial Chamber erred in holding that this was a peripheral matter. It is not, Mr. President. Now, accordingly, now that we have this issue of coded telegrams associated with Drago Nikolic's intent, I think it is important that I come back quickly on the pattern of telephone calls which were made in this case because Drago Nikolic has been associated with these telephone calls. As a matter of fact, the Trial Chamber at paragraph 509 stated that there was such a pattern of telephone calls. That was in dealing with the issue of the 2nd Battalion and Acimovic. I'd just like to mention briefly, Mr. President, that three battalions receive such telephone calls related to the arrival of prisoners, at least three that we know of. The 4th Battalion, located in Orahovac, I refer to transcript 10062, would have received a telegram on 14 July, and that is Lazar Ristic -- not a telegram, I apologise, a phone conversation. And the phone conversation came from Trbic, who asked Lazar Ristic to send some men over to provide security at the school because there was problems with prisoners who wanted to escape. The second telephone conversation we are aware of happened with the 6th Battalion, and that was also on 14 July, and is related in the testimony of Marko Milosevic and Ostoja Stanisic. And that is at transcript 13300-13301. And they say that Jokic, the duty officer, and not Nikolic called them to inform them to inform them of the arrival of the prisoners at Petkovci school. The third battalion which reserved [sic] a call and a telegram, which, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, was not coded is the 1st Battalion and that is found of course in the testimony of Slavko Peric, which can be found at 11375, transcript, 11376. And this -- what you will find in this transcript is that Mr. Pelemis, the deputy commander of the battalion, met with his command staff at the battalion and he basically said that there was someone from the brigade who had called and that they had to go to the school. My colleague mentioned that earlier this week. I will not come back to what was mentioned concerning this telephone conversation. The issue I want to raise, however, Mr. President, is that when we look at the alleged pattern of phone calls, the pattern is such that, one, there is no coded telegram, which helps in determining the issue of Acimovic and the 2nd Battalion; and two, the pattern of telephone calls really, when associated with Drago Nikolic, is not an element that will be of any assistance to you, we submit respectfully, in determining his intent. The Prosecution - and I'm always on my preliminary matter - also mentions in its brief reply and again today what happened at Orahovac. And at paragraph 252 of its appeal brief, the Prosecution raises the issue of the execution site, saying, and I quote: "Nikolic and Popovic told the soldiers what to do." Now, that's at the execution site. Now, with respect to this finding of the Chamber at paragraph 252, I wish to place on the record two decisions. Mr. President, can we move into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I now move to the first question posed by the Appeals Chamber, and this question deals of course with our submission that the Prosecution exceeded its notice of appeal in the arguments presented in its appeals brief. I'll be very short on this one, Mr. President. Although we do believe that technically we are right and that the Prosecution should not have exceeded its notice of appeal, and although we believe it was inappropriate for the Prosecution to, in a reply to which Mr. Nikolic has no standing to raise any submission in a reply, to ask for its notice of appeal to be amended pursuant to Rule 108. Nonetheless, Mr. President, considering that the Appeals Chamber will necessarily have to consider the generally accepted factors which the Prosecution -- in order to consider whether the Prosecution has met its burden to show that no other reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded that -- the conclusion that Drago Nikolic possessed the necessary mens rea for genocide is not the only reasonable inference available. We do not intend to pursue this issue any further. I now move to ground 7 of the Prosecution or seventh ground of appeal. At paragraph 1407, the Trial Chamber found the following that: "Soon after the inception of his involvement in the killing operation and certainly by the time of executions at Orahovac, Nikolic knew that this was a massive killing operation being carried out with a genocidal intent." Of course, Mr. President, the Appeals Chamber knows very well that we are challenging this finding, but let me just go on for the time being. Considering that the -- sorry, the Trial Chamber then held as follows immediately following this paragraph: "Having considered and weighed all of the above factors, individually and cumulatively, the Trial Chamber is not satisfied that the only reasonable inference to be drawn from Nikolic's act is that he shared the genocidal intent." The Trial Chamber went on to say in the same paragraph a little later that: "In these circumstances, the stringent test for specific intent is not met and the Trial Chamber therefore finds that Nikolic did not participate in the JCE to murder with genocidal intent." Now, of course, the key words here, Mr. President, are "intent is not the only reasonable inference." And before I go on, I draw the attention of the Appeals Chamber to the fact that of course the Prosecution has the burden to show that this was not the only reasonable inference, and that we say, based on what they argued this morning, amongst other things, the fact that when Drago Nikolic chose to act with resolve and purpose, that would have been sufficient according to the Prosecution, we say it is absolutely not sufficient. Now, we all know, Mr. President, that an inference drawn from circumstantial evidence to establish a fact, especially on which a conviction relies, that inference must be the only reasonable one that could be drawn from the evidence presented. That of course Stakic appeal, paragraph 219. This is significant, in our view, because, as held by the Trial Chamber, direct evidence of genocide, intent, is rare; instead, it must be inferred from the acts, the conduct, knowledge of the accused, as well as from other relevant circumstances, judgement 1398. In this case, Mr. President, in addition to finding that Drago Nikolic did not harbour genocidal intent because this is not the only reasonable inference which could be drawn, the Trial Chamber actually went further and identified another reasonable inference available on the basis of the evidence. The Trial Chamber held the following: "Another reasonable inference is that Nikolic's blind dedication to the security service led him to doggedly pursue the efficient execution of his assigned task in this operation." Now, in fact, Mr. President, not only is this inference not the only reasonable one available on the basis of the evidence, there are even other reasonable inferences that can be drawn and I'll get back to this later in my argument. We submit, Mr. President, that the Prosecution failed to demonstrate - and that is the answer of course to the second question posed by the Appeals Chamber - that it failed to show that considering the Trial Chamber's error whether there would be a change to the Trial Chamber's conclusion, that it is not the only reasonable inference that can be drawn that Drago Nikolic harboured genocidal intent. My argument will be presented in four sections. I will first begin with the fact that the Trial Chamber did consider all generally accepted factors related to genocidal intent; secondly, the Trial Chamber correctly considered all appropriate factors and the Prosecution failed to show an error on behalf of the Trial Chamber. I will move on to explore with the Appeals Chamber the lack of contextual knowledge of Drago Nikolic, and I will conclude by what we figure or what we respectfully submit is the determining criteria in this regard. Moving on to the generally accepted factors related to genocidal intent, contrary to the Prosecution's submission the Chamber did consider all generally accepted factors. On this basis, the Trial Chamber rightly found that Drago Nikolic did not entertain the required mens rea for genocide. Our detailed argument can be found in our response brief at paragraphs 28 to 34. The Prosecution simply did not succeed in showing that the Trial Chamber erred. At paragraphs 823, the Trial Chamber specifically stated that the generally accepted factors from which an intent to destroy may be inferred, of course in the absence of direct evidence. These factors, Mr. President, were used with Beara, they were used with Popovic, and they were used with Nikolic, albeit commensurate with their acts based on the findings of the Chamber. Secondly, and more importantly, Mr. President, contrary to the Prosecution's argument, it stems from the Trial Chamber's finding that not a single general accepted factor was left out. And let's explore together, if you want, Mr. President, some of these findings. The Trial Chamber did consider the scale and scope of the killing operation, that is, at judgement 1405. In fact, the Trial Chamber went further. It considered the lack of Drago Nikolic's involvement in many aspects of the operation leading to the conclusion that he was unaware of the full scale and scope. That is judgement 1402-1403, 1410, 1412. The Trial Chamber considered Drago Nikolic's contribution to the JCE after learning of the others' genocidal intent, judgement 1407. Once again, the Trial Chamber went further. It considered the limited scope of his involvement, judgement 1402-1403 and 1410 to 1412. The Trial Chamber also considered that Drago Nikolic witnessed the targeting of Bosnian Muslims, judgement 1404. However, the Trial Chamber also considered Drago Nikolic's belief that prisoners, as opposed to any other description of victims, were being brought in to the Zvornik area, judgement 1402-1403, and that not every prisoner would be executed. Now, of course this applies to the prisoners from the Milici hospital, and that is judgement at paragraph 1411. The Trial Chamber considered the repetitive nature of Drago Nikolic's action, holding that Nikolic's act and participation did provide some evidence of a genocidal intent on his part or from which such an intent could be inferred, judgement paragraph 1409. However, the Trial Chamber also considered the limited temporal scope of his acts and his withdrawal from the criminal acts prior to their completion. Of course I'm referring here, at the minimum, to what happened in Branjevo Farm and the Pilica cultural centre, judgement 1410. The Trial Chamber also considered Drago Nikolic's perpetration of cruel and inhumane treatment, judgement 1408, 1425. But the Trial Chamber also considered his lack of responsibility for very important aspects of the genocidal operation, such as the killings at Kravica warehouse, the killings of the Milici hospital patients, the reburial operation, and others, judgement 1402-1403 and 1411. The Trial Chamber considered Drago Nikolic's intent for the underlying crimes in light of his membership in the alleged JCE to kill, judgement 1403. But, again, at the same time, the Trial Chamber also considered that Drago Nikolic was not involved in the forcible transfer and his corresponding lack of intent for an important component of the genocide. Just in this specific regard, Mr. President, I'd like to bring the attention of the Trial [sic] Chamber to the indictment because the indictment defined the genocide as including four components, and we believe that this is important when you consider those four components in drawing whether the inference of genocidal intent can be drawn when you look at his participation in the overall genocidal acts as charged in the indictment. The forcible transfer, by the way, was at judgement 1395 and 1402-1403. Regarding the use of derogatory language, the Trial Chamber, contrary to what the Prosecution advances, specifically addressed this issue, holding that while the use of derogatory language may be of relevance in relation to genocidal intent, it does not in and of itself evidence such intent. And the Trial Chamber goes on in saying this is particularly the case, given the culture in the VRS and the Zvornik Brigade, in which such language was commonplace. Now, the Trial Chamber also considered -- sorry, this was 1399, judgement. The Trial Chamber considered the general context in which Drago Nikolic's acts occurred, 1402, judgement. The Trial Chamber goes further and also considers his belated entry into the JCE and his limited contextual knowledge, and that's one of the issues I'll come back to. The judgement -- that was at 1402 to 1403. Concerning the existence of a plan, this was also considered by the Trial Chamber at 1403-1404. Strikingly, the Trial Chamber also considered that Drago Nikolic was not involved in the inception of the plan and was never fully informed in this respect, judgement 1402 to 1404. It necessarily follows in our submission, Mr. President, that all nine factors invoked by the Prosecution were indeed considered by the Trial Chamber and that the Prosecution failed to establish any error on the part of the Trial Chamber. Second part of my argument, contrary to the Prosecution's assertion, the Trial Chamber applied correct law and accurately weighed all appropriate factors related to Drago Nikolic's intent. Firstly, it is incorrect to say that the Trial Chamber assessed Drago Nikolic's genocidal intent based on what he could have done instead of what he did. That's incorrect. To begin with, it is very well accepted that in assessing genocidal intent, a Trial Chamber must consider the totality of the evidence, including the non-involvement or the absence of involvement of an accused, that can be found in Stakic appeal judgement 5245 -- sorry, this is -- I might have a problem here with the -- I have a four-digit paragraph which cannot be. I'll come back to that, Mr. President. Now, the key here is the Trial Chamber's finding that Popovic and Beara were the architects of the plan, while Drago Nikolic, and here I quote, "... was brought in to carry out specific tasks assigned to him in implementation of a monstrous plan designed by others." Judgement 1410. The Trial Chamber correctly found that the acts were confined, the acts -- of course Drago Nikolic's act were confined to his area of responsibility, and thus that his participation and role in the operation was not overarching, as demonstrated by his non-involvement in important aspects. It follows, Mr. President, that the Trial Chamber considered both what Drago Nikolic did as well as what Drago Nikolic could have done, all of which in our submission is relevant. Secondly, it isn't correct to say that the Trial Chamber unreasonably demanded that Nikolic's participation in criminal acts that were completed before his joining the genocide. For starters, this fails to take into account the Prosecution's own allegations in the indictment charging Drago Nikolic with many acts committed outside of Zvornik, including of course the forcible transfer. In our view, the Chamber was right in considering the fact that Drago Nikolic was involved in these acts -- the fact that he was not involved in these acts a relevant factor. More importantly, the Prosecution's argument ignores that Drago Nikolic's non-participation in the events which took place before the JCE are directly related to his lack of contextual knowledge. Again, I'll come back to this later. Now, the Prosecution did not reply here to this -- when we responded on this specific issue. There's no reply from the Prosecution. Thirdly, it isn't correct to say that the Trial Chamber contradicted its own findings. This is a quick one. Clearly, not much needs to be said, as there are no contradictions. You can verify, Mr. President, the paragraphs advanced by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber correctly found that Drago Nikolic did not take part in the transfer of prisoners, as he was not involved in the JCE to forcibly transfer the prisoners. Fourthly, it isn't correct to say that the Trial Chamber erred, finding that Nikolic's involvement in the unarmed detention of the Milici hospital patients further negate Nikolic's intent. Now, even before I go into the substance of this statement which we say isn't correct, it is important, Mr. President, to bear in mind one thing: It is not for the -- for Mr. Nikolic to show that he does not have genocidal intent. So we're not talking about a factor that will negate his intent. What the Prosecution must bring forward is the factors that do establish his intent. They have the burden of reversing the inference drawn by the Trial Chamber. Now, in this specific instance about the Milici hospital patients, at paragraph 1380, the Trial Chamber found that: "There is scant evidence as to the precise circumstances of their murder and even less evidence as to what, if any, the role of Nikolic had in the matter." The Prosecution claimed that Drago Nikolic would have allowed the prisoners to be taken away and murdered. This must be firmly rejected. The Trial Chamber found that Drago Nikolic had a role in the custody, and thus that he had an opportunity to further the genocidal plan by arranging himself for their execution. Yet, they remained safe within the custody of Nikolic and the Zvornik Brigade and they were killed only after Popovic took control of them, judgement 1411. The Prosecution's contention that Drago Nikolic's involvement in the murder was a result of the timing of the superior order for their execution must also be dismissed. The fact of the matter remains that the prisoners remained safe within the custody of Nikolic. The Trial Chamber, in our view, Mr. President, correctly considered Nikolic's subordinate role, contrary of course to the Prosecution's argument. As previously mentioned, Drago Nikolic acted or acts must be considered in the context of the evidence in totality. And, to that end, Nikolic's personal circumstances are very relevant: The fact that he is a second lieutenant; the fact that this is the lowest rank in the army; the fact that he didn't attend any military academy; the fact that the position he was holding was a position for someone of a rank at least three ranks higher than his. In the context of an operation, of course, directed, according to the Trial Chamber, by Popovic and Beara, he had little authority of his own. As mentioned -- referred to specifically by the Trial Chamber, the evidence provided by Pandurevic that Nikolic was wearing a coat much too big for him. How is this relevant, Mr. President? Well, simply because the determination that Nikolic did not have genocidal intent because the fact that he had little authority of his own could very well provide other reasons justifying his actions, other than the fact that he harboured genocidal intent. The Trial Chamber also did not err in law or in fact in considering Drago Nikolic's dedication to the security service. Now, here again, Mr. President, I pause because this is actually not a finding. This is actually another reasonable inference, and this, in our view, is different from a finding. The Trial Chamber did not confuse intent and motive, rather it correctly applied the burden of proof in relation to inferences regarding the mens rea of an accused. In conclusion on this second topic, Mr. President, it follows from the above, even if the Appeals Chamber was to take into consideration the alleged errors committed by the Trial Chamber in determining Nikolic's mens rea for genocide, Nikolic's specific intent would not be unequivocally established. Why? Because genocidal intent on the part of Drago Nikolic is not the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. And I move to my third part, which is the lack of contextual knowledge, but before I do so I'd like to come back quickly to something which was stated by the Trial Chamber, citing the Krstic appeal judgement, where the Trial Chamber quoted the following paragraph 37, appeals judgement Krstic: "The gravity of genocide is reflected in the stringent requirements which must be satisfied before this conviction is imposed. In this context, the demanding proof of specific intent is one of the safe-guards to ensure that convictions for this crime will not be imposed lightly." These requirements, Mr. President, guard against a danger that convictions for this crime will be entered or imposed lightly. This is Krstic appeal judgement, paragraph 37, and cited by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 1408. The Trial Chamber properly identified this danger in paragraph 1408, and therefore acted with caution when determining whether the genocidal intent on the part of Drago Nikolic was indeed the only reasonable inference. The Trial Chamber concluded that it was not, and we say that the Appeals Chamber should follow in the footsteps of the Trial Chamber in applying the same degree of care. I move to my third argument which has to do with the lack of contextual knowledge. I said at the beginning that it is our submission that Drago Nikolic was not aware of a genocidal intent; however, even if he was aware of genocidal intent, the contextual knowledge is also something that must be considered. At paragraph 237 of its appellant's brief, the Prosecution submits that Nikolic's actions and participation in the genocide, with full knowledge of the genocidal aims of the operation and that of his fellow JCE members, Popovic and Beara, evidence his genocidal intent. Well, we say, Mr. President, that this must be considered in the light of the Trial Chamber's holding that genocidal intent, in the absence of direct evidence, must be inferred from the acts, the conduct, the knowledge, as well as other relevant circumstances. Judgement 1398, quoted earlier. Consequently, Mr. President, while knowledge of the genocidal aim of the operation or that of others is a relevant consideration to assess intent, so is the contextual knowledge of the accused. And the contextual knowledge refers to the full spectrum of the knowledge of the accused which necessarily has a bearing on his understanding of the situation and, accordingly, on his actions. In this case, Drago Nikolic's lack of contextual knowledge is a determining factor. Let us recall a few of the Trial Chamber's findings. Drago Nikolic was first informed of the murder plan on the evening of 13 July. Now, I say these findings, of course, without prejudice to our arguments that many of these findings are challenged in our appeal. In the evening of 13 July -- and that the information he was given was sparse, a large number of prisoners were being brought from Bratunac to Zvornik to be executed. By that time, the murder operation was well underway, judgement 1402. The vast majority of the victims had already been detained. Over 1.000 victims had already been or were about to be executed at Kravica warehouse and Sandici meadow. This was at judgement 1402. We could add what happened the executions at Cerska. On the evidence before the Trial Chamber, Nikolic had no knowledge of those events, other than his general understanding that these were prisoners taken as a result of the attack on and fall of the Srebrenica enclave. He had no information as to the circumstances by which these men had ended up in VRS custody. He did not know about the indiscriminate separations in Potocari and he did not know about the vigorous pursuit of victims on the Konjevic Polje road. It follows, Mr. President, that even through Drago Nikolic was likely aware of the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July, he was not aware of the adoption of any plan by anyone to murder the able-bodied men from Srebrenica who had been separated from their families, judgement 1051. Moreover, Drago Nikolic might have had some information concerning the column of people from Srebrenica, which was no way -- it's -- which was on its way, of course, to Konjevic Polje and then headed towards Tuzla - and we know the information in the evidence in relation to this column - but he had no information concerning the composition of the column. More importantly, he had no information concerning the presence of civilians in this column, nor did he have information concerning the ongoing operation to capture members of the column. What he did know, however, is the fact that a significant component of the column was on its way to the area of Zvornik and that this column was armed. In addition to this, there is little, if any, evidence, Mr. President, of any working or close working relationship between Nikolic and Popovic or Beara before 13 July 1995. And of course Drago Nikolic had no direct involvement with the prisoners prior to that time, judgement 1402. The fact that Drago Nikolic had no knowledge of these events is, in our view, highly significant. Even if the Trial Chamber's finding that Drago Nikolic knew the genocidal intent -- genocidal aim of the operation or that of others, even though if that was to be affirmed by the Appeals Chamber, when you look at Drago Nikolic's lack of contextual knowledge, it makes it possible to draw another reasonable inference, other than the one identified by the Trial Chamber. For example, Mr. President, another reasonable inference that can be drawn on the basis of the totality of the evidence is that Drago Nikolic due, amongst other things, to his low rank, lack of training, lack of power of influence and little authority of his own, was drawn into an operation much bigger than him in which he had no other option but to contribute, but that he was nonetheless able to extract himself from at the earliest opportunity. The most important factor supporting the Trial Chamber's inference concerning Drago Nikolic, last part of my argument today. Most important factor, Mr. President, is the fact that Drago Nikolic did not harbour genocidal intent is that his contribution to the killing operation ended abruptly after 36 hours. Genocidal intent is not a switch that you can flick on or off at pleasure, nor is it an intent that you can have for one day and not have it the next. The fact that as of 15 July in the morning Drago Nikolic no longer contributed to the killing operation is the most powerful indicator that he never had genocidal intent. Genocidal intent, Mr. President, cannot be established through a series of inferences. We are talking about a person that will be tagged with having genocidal intent. The burden or the threshold of the burden of proof must be very high. That is why, as mentioned earlier, the gravity of genocide is reflected in the stringent requirement that before this conviction can be imposed, specific intent must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Mr. President, I will stop here and simply end my argument by saying that based on the totality of the evidence in this case when the Appeals Chamber analyses all of the evidence, and of course with all the findings that we are challenging concerning Orahovac and the presence at the execution site, concerning Rocevic and the fact that this conversation never took place, concerning the fact that he never offered uniforms, all of this put together, there will be no doubt in your mind, Mr. President, that this inference -- it's certainly the inference that the Prosecution would like to say, that he had -- that Drago Nikolic had the specific intent is certainly not the only one. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Counsel for Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you just give me a few minutes to set myself up. Thank you. Good afternoon. The Prosecution appeals in the case of Vinko Pandurevic, in our submission, raise no true issues of law. They are, in reality, a request for a review of the evidence by the Appeals Chamber, and the irony of the Prosecution's approach to these appeals and cross-appeals will not escape the Chamber's attention, whereas in the case of those substantially convicted it seeks to uphold as reasonable the findings of the Trial Chamber. In the case of Pandurevic, it seeks a complete revision of the central factual findings, sufficient not just to correct a minor legal error, but rather completely to relitigate almost every charge of which he has been acquitted. On behalf of Vinko Pandurevic, I respectfully remind the Chamber of the strict standard of review of Trial Chamber findings of fact on appeal, namely, that no Trial Chamber could have found such facts. I was giving that concept some thought the other day when it occurred to me what a steep gradient it truly is, because what it really means is that you can't think of any two Judges who would agree with the finding of the Trial Chamber. And why do I say that? Well, a Trial Chamber, as we know in the case of Vinko Pandurevic, can make a decision by majority of two to one. And so, if you find yourself thinking: Well, I do actually know a couple of Judges who might agree with that, then that standard will not have been met. It makes it rather interesting if there are two among you who would support a finding of fact but three disagree. I would submit it would be extraordinary for the majority to overrule the minority in those circumstances because you have necessarily identified the component of a Trial Chamber which would have found that fact. As I say, it's a steep gradient to invite a Chamber on appeal to re-write the factual findings of a Trial Chamber below, and more so, I submit, for the Prosecution because not only does it have to satisfy you that no Trial Chamber could have found a fact, it has to satisfy you now that you could be sure that that fact should be found. Mr. Rogers the other day made some statistical observations to you. I'm not going to repeat them. This was a case which lasted the best part of three years. It generated an enormous amount of transcript. There were many, many witnesses, thousands of exhibits, and if I may pause just to say this because I know an English court of appeal would observe to me that, Mr. Haynes, this was a very experienced Judge. Your Honours, this was a very experienced Chamber. It composed -- it comprised the current Vice-President and immediate Vice-President of this Tribunal and in Judge Prost, one of its most respected jurists. They managed the proceedings admirably, they managed the case throughout very well. They were attentive, they watched the evidence, they wrote a concise, considered, and eloquent judgement. I just want to make a few observations whilst I'm talking about this on some of the things you've heard today. The Trial Chamber, for example, heard far more detailed evidence as to who was doing what and how they came to be at the crime sites. I didn't object today to the use by the Prosecution of maps with arrows on them. Doubtless, that was a useful visual aid for you, but please bear in mind what underlines those graphic -- underlies those graphic images. Simply to characterise them as Zvornik Brigade assets or resources is oversimplistic. You need to know what they were, how they were -- got there, and what they did there. Just by way of example, paragraph 1881 of the judgement was cited by the Prosecution as justification for one of the arrows on the maps this morning. But an examination of the judgement reveals only that some soldiers cleared some bodies from outside a school building because the local villagers asked them to do it. It's no indication at all that those men were acting regularly within their capacity as members of a battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. Secondly, that the Chamber heard a wealth of evidence about Pandurevic's military capabilities within the brigade, what units and artillery he had at his disposal, and in -- particularly, the heavy artillery with which he could have crushed the column or even murdered it as it passed by, in particular it heard from PW-168 whose evidence it so readily championed on this topic. Such evidence was central to the Chamber's findings about the passage of the column at Baljkovica and how it stood to Pandurevic's credit and how it helped them determine his intent to participate in any joint criminal enterprise or criminal scheme. More importantly, perhaps most importantly of all, in a case in which a man's culpability turns on a single conversation, the Trial Chamber heard from PW-168 for 18 whole days and Pandurevic for 22. However they may have articulated Pandurevic's knowledge on the 15th of July in the judgement and whether or whether not the expressions they used were consistent or slightly different, they articulated that -- I'm sorry, the knowledge he derived from a conversation that could have lasted no more than a few seconds, they were ideally and uniquely placed to gauge in a way which, with respect, Your Honours are not. I just want to say a few words about Vinko Pandurevic. In July of 1995 he was 35 years of age and married with one daughter. He became the commander of the Zvornik Brigade in 1993, aged 33. He was well beneath the expected age to be a brigade commander and well below the rank that one would expect a brigade commander to be. He was nonetheless regarded as a fine soldier. The Zvornik Brigade was a unit of 5 and a half thousand men, two or three times the size of an ordinary brigade, and as you've seen from the schematics this morning it comprised eight battalions which were spread along a front line about 40 kilometres in length. The soldiers were substantially non-professional. This was, after all, a time of civil war when ethnic groups were fighting each other. The 1st Battalion, quite literally, were a farming unit. You're not going to get the opportunity which the Trial Chamber had of hearing from Vinko Pandurevic, as they did for the best part of a month, during which time every conceivable question was put to him by me and five other parties, including the Prosecution. It's axiomatic to say that the determination of his case was substantially shaped by the evidence he gave, so I'm therefore going to try my best to do justice to the case he advanced and which was substantially accepted. I promise it won't take me 22 days. We all agree that prior to the 15th of July, 1995, Vinko Pandurevic had no knowledge whatsoever of the murder plan. That has seemed therefore the natural starting point for any narrative; however, it's perhaps worth just backing up a little. The movement of the prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik began on the 13th of July. It is universally acknowledged that the original plan had been to murder them in Bratunac, but Deronjic objected. The prisoners were moved to Zvornik during the night of the 13th of July and during the day of the 14th. They were transported and guarded by substantial resources drawn from the Bratunac Brigade and other units. At noon on the 15th of July, Vinko Pandurevic returned to the brigade headquarters in Karakaj after an absence of two weeks. He knew that there was a serious military situation developing with a large enemy force behind his front lines commonly called the column, and there were also enemy attacks from the front. What we're all agreed about now is that he had not a clue as he pushed the door open of the Standard Barracks that somebody had brought a number of prisoners to the Zvornik municipality, detained them in schools and some other buildings, and was killing them. The first person he met was his deputy or Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic, who held a brief conversation with him in the corridor. He is characterised throughout the Prosecution's submissions as the Chief of Staff, as though that is some key to his knowledge. Formally he was the Chief of Staff; however, Obrenovic had been absent from the brigade throughout the 14th of July until about an hour previously. Accordingly, the information he had was very limited and it derived almost exclusively from a brief exchange with the duty officer, Dragan Jokic. What he, in fact, said, the Trial Chamber found, was: Pursuant to Mladic's order, Beara and Popovic had brought a large number of prisoners from Bratunac to the Zvornik sector, where they were executing them. And Jokic had informed him that there were enormous problems with the guarding, execution, and burial of prisoners. Significantly, what Obrenovic knew and didn't say was that Nikolic was involved or that Beara and Popovic were taking whomever they want wherever they want, which Jokic had just told him. There it is. We can't go behind what PW-168 told us about that conversation. That is the only evidence and the Trial Chamber accepted it. It must have shocked Vinko Pandurevic. He didn't even know prisoners had been taken, let alone brought to the area, and the Trial Chamber significantly found no significance in his response about civil protection. Know well also his immediate concern with his formal orders to block the column and Obrenovic's alarming report in that regard, conveying to him that the situation was serious. The other thing Obrenovic's report cannot have failed to indicate to him was that the operation he was referring to was one being conducted by the Main Staff. The name of Beara would necessarily have alerted him to that. Shortly afterwards, they entered a room, where together with police and other military commanders, they discussed how to fulfil their orders to block and destroy the column of combatants behind their lines. Is the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 1972 about what Vinko Pandurevic would have known from that conversation thus not reasonable? That that's all he was told, that's all his knowledge can be based upon. Jokic was the duty officer. Pandurevic would know that from his contact with the brigade that morning and his entry into the building. Indeed, he even gave evidence about that. The suggestion now that the mention of Jokic's name would necessarily trigger some understanding that the brigade was involved in burials is not the only possible inference, though I accept the contents of the report he wrote later. Pandurevic is criticised for his inaction in the light of this skeletal information from somebody whom himself did not know very much, namely, Obrenovic. Indeed, it is said that his inaction from that point as a commander makes him guilty of a joint criminal enterprise. Certainly, the Prosecution, nor anybody, can point to any positive act by Pandurevic at any time, let alone after noon on July the 15th. And if he were, as it were, to have responded in any other way, then we would know about it. If he had been told prior to that, we would know about it. One compelling piece of evidence which the Trial Chamber heard and which I'll invite you quickly to look at is an intercept, it's P1179, it's conveniently set out at paragraph 1282 of the trial judgement. It's a lengthy intercept and it takes place earlier that morning and the participants in the conversation are Beara, who is somewhere in the Zvornik area, and Krstic, who is at the front line command post near Zepa. You will recall that at 9.00 that morning, Krstic had ordered Pandurevic to return to Zvornik to crush the column. It is shortly after that that Beara contacted Krstic at the command post. Beara is, throughout the course of the conversation, making it plain that he is having difficulty dealing with the murder plan in the Zvornik area, and he discusses with Krstic the various possibilities for the provision of men and other resources to complete the task. A number of possibilities are discussed between them, including men from a unit commanded by Bobo Indic and men from the Bratunac Brigade. What of course is conspicuously absent from this conversation is any suggestion that Beara in Zvornik should turn to the Zvornik Brigade to ask them for any resource. That simply is not on the table and it's an indication, we say, of the extent to which Pandurevic was kept always in the dark about this Main Staff and Drina Corps operation. During the course of that afternoon, Pandurevic was visited at the forward command post by a local politician called Branko Grujic, and Grujic was who told him about the presence of prisoners in a couple of schools. And, hence, in his later interim combat report is featured the mention of schools. There were in that conversation indications that the local population were insecure about the presence of the prisoners there, and so Pandurevic decided to consult further with a man called Ljubo Bojanovic who was present at the forward command post to find out what he knew about the prisoners. Bojanovic told him that a day previously buses had passed by the command in Karakaj containing prisoners. He said he thought they were on their way to Bijeljina, that is the place where the exchange centre of Batkovici is, and that the brigade had no task in relation to the prisoners. What Pandurevic did next is, we say, very significant. He knew from earlier that morning that the commander of the Muslim forces in Nezuk, Semso Muminovic, had been trying to make contact with him, and it was at that point that Pandurevic contacted Muminovic. He contacted him several times that afternoon, and the Trial Chamber accepted his evidence at paragraph 1867. The contact began at about 2.00 in the afternoon, very shortly after Pandurevic had arrived at the forward command post. There is in the evidence in fact a record of one of their conversations, and I think we'll just have a look at this on the screen, it's 7D00656. No, I only want the transcript. There's no point in playing the audio. Thank you. The English is at the lower half. This is Pandurevic on the early afternoon of the 15th of July, contacting Muminovic, whom he refers to as Zukov, his nickname. In his evidence he described this as the second conversation and you'll see that Pandurevic says: "From that ... there's no." Zukov says: "Good, good." Pandurevic says: "Zukov, Zukov, Zukov, answer me." And Zukov says: "Speak, I hear you. I hear you. Speak. He's not answering me. "Zukov, send the civilians to one place, choose it yourself. We will transport them all to Tuzla. This way they will be protected certainly, copy. Zukov: "Well, let the whole column pass and it's all right." Pandurevic: "Not with weaponry, it has to be surrendered, not with weaponry, I won't repeat twice, so that they also have the chance to gather at the same place. Copy!" The military necessity on which the Prosecution have always relied did not exist at the time of this contact with the enemy commander, didn't arise until the morning of the 16th of July. And literally within an hour or so of arriving back in Zvornik, having got to the forward command post, Pandurevic is making contact with the ABiH commander in Nezuk, starting negotiations for the passage of the column of men to safe territory. It is unsurprising, we submit, that the Trial Chamber formed the view that this was compelling evidence to negate any suggestion that Pandurevic had merely by being given information by Obrenovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- become a member of any joint criminal enterprise to murder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, sorry, we will break in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The negotiations continued and you'll see at paragraph 1872 of the judgement the following morning a Muslim officer from the column called Selikovic [phoen] was taken prisoner. He was treated and he was sent back to his unit. Again, an example of humane treatment, inconsistent with any intent or contribution to a joint criminal enterprise to murder. At 10.00, Pandurevic and Muminovic agreed the opening of the corridor, and at 1.00 it was opened. I'll return to this point later, but I do submit that that act as a piece of evidence in determining Pandurevic's deeds and thoughts and what inference the Trial Chamber must have drawn is fantastically compelling. Do not underestimate, we say, the significance of the disobedience of the order he had been given to crush the column. That had come from Mladic through Krstic. This was the column of the 28th Division. This was the unit that had been the thorn in the side of the whole VRS in Srebrenica. Pandurevic had the military capability to wipe it out and he chose not to. Your Honour, that may be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll break for 20 minutes, that's 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just complete the story of the column. The column was originally open for a period of 24 hours, but because there was stragglers, Pandurevic kept it open for a further period, sent his men out into the area around Baljkovica with megaphones to make sure that as many people got through as was possible, and it's estimated that about 10.000 people passed through. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 1964 that in his interim combat report of the 15th of July, Pandurevic was preparing to disobey his orders, and I simply note within the time-scale of things that that is within five and a half hours of his arrival back at Zvornik and no more than four from his arrival at the forward command post. And the Trial Chamber was satisfied that by then he had that in mind. On the 16th of July he wrote what can only be described as a dishonest report, lying to his superior command, attesting to the fact that he was still fighting when he wasn't and saying that some people had slipped through but they were unarmed. That was quite the opposite of the position because he was letting the whole Muslim column pass through, contrary to his orders. Two days later when, as the Trial Chamber found, he was fixed with rather more complete knowledge of what had been going on with the murder operation, he wrote the interim combat report of the 18th of July, and I will read that to you. It said: "During the last ten days or so, the municipality of Zvornik has been swamped with Srebrenica Turks. It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality in addition to the 7.000 or so who had fled into the forests. This has created an extremely complex situation and the possibility of the total occupation of Zvornik in conjunction with the forces at the front. These actions have stirred up great discontent among the people and the general opinion is that Zvornik is to pay the price for the taking of Srebrenica." Concurrently to that, he ordered the Zvornik Brigade to ensure that all prisoners taken on the terrain were brought back to the barracks, and you'll find that at paragraph 1893 of the judgement. The reports which he wrote firstly to prepare his higher command for the passage of the column and then condemning them for the murder operation were described in these words by Judge Kwon in his dissenting opinion. He said: "They were the sole instance of a subordinate so openly challenging Mladic in relation to the murder operation. I would add this, they are the sole instance of any document recording the existence of prisoners rather than referring to them in some sort of secretive code." This material also the Trial Chamber in our submission rightly felt was relevant to determine the purpose of his acts and deeds and his involvement in the murder operation. Throughout the 20th to the 24th of July he took and exchanged prisoners at a time when for -- in other regions such as Bratunac, prisoners were being routinely executed. On the 27th of July, he visited his command superior General Krstic, the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 1915, and asked Krstic if he had any more specific information following his combat reports relating to the prisoners executed in Zvornik area. According to Pandurevic, Krstic essentially told him that it was not something that should be his concern and that he would deal with the problem anyway. On those facts as described by the narrative and attested to by Pandurevic in evidence on oath, the Trial Chamber perfectly reasonably concluded not only that Pandurevic's actions throughout the 30 hours from noon on the 15th of July were not consistent with his membership of the JCE nor as an aider and abettor to mass murder. Neither did they consider that his actions in writing reports or letting the column go had to be viewed with the cynicism that the Prosecution now invites. Quite the contrary, in relation to the column they found the following: "At the time in which other VRS members were actively hunting down, capturing, and executing Bosnian Muslim men without mercy and pursuing the genocidal claim, Pandurevic's decision to open the corridor enabled the safe passage of thousands of Bosnian Muslim men is striking. In doing so, thousands of men were potentially spared. Pandurevic's action in this regard stands out as an instance of courage and humanity in a period typified by human weakness, cruelty, and depravity." Plainly, they were not regarded by the Trial Chamber in the same way, even after the Prosecution had cross-examined him for hours as self-serving or corroboration of his having accepted Mladic's illegal order. In our submission, it would be quite wrong of you to reverse those factual findings. Under the Prosecution's first ground of appeal, we submit that the alleged actus reus for the joint criminal enterprise is little more than a linguistic sophistry. He did not accept Mladic's order, he did not give any orders in relation to the murder operation, he did not approve any orders, he didn't sanction the use of any resources or assets, and he did not know they were being used such as they were. I'll turn now to the appeal under Article 7(3). It is our position that the correct standard of knowledge for a superior is that he has to have reason to know that his subordinates have committed, are committing, or are about to commit crimes. But we accept that the terminology has become fuzzy and vague and we would welcome clarification in this case. However, even under the lower standard of Strugar and Nahimana we contend that the Trial Chamber was perfectly entitled to conclude that they were not sure that Vinko Pandurevic was liable under Article 7(3) for extermination and persecution, and I will briefly underline why. Extermination, this deals with the second question which we've been asked to address. Essentially, these questions come back and back and back again to the conversation between Pandurevic and Obrenovic in the corridor of the Standard Barracks on the 15th of July, and we ask rhetorically: What was it about what Obrenovic told him that would have made him think that this was extermination or persecution. Pandurevic's knowledge about the scopes of the crimes underway was skeletal in the light of what he was told by Obrenovic. He had no information whatsoever as to the numbers of prisoners brought to the area or even their approximate location. He had no knowledge as to whether they were all being killed or just some of them were being killed, nor as to whether the executions were complete, over, or ongoing. All of those are facts emerged later. The Trial Chamber found out that Pandurevic only learned of the full scope of the operation on the 18th of July. He did not know at that time that extermination was being committed. The use of the word "enormous," moreover does not lead to the necessary inference -- influence that that is invited. There may have been enormous logistical problems getting somebody to carry out the tasks, for example, and so we submit that the brief conversation with Obrenovic was correctly characterised by the Trial Chamber, as only giving rise to the necessary influence that Pandurevic would have known of murder but not necessarily extermination. Can I turn to the third question you have posed us about persecution. Again, I'm sorry to say it involves an analysis of the information passed from Obrenovic to Pandurevic on the 15th of July. Nothing in that information could have conveyed to Pandurevic the reasons why prisoners were being killed. He would not have known from what Obrenovic said that they were being killed because of their ethnicity rather than, for example, what they might have done or for some arbitrary reason, in other words, revenge, or because some -- simply they were enemy soldiers. The conversation with Obrenovic does not relay that information in any way at all. It's important also, given that the information was passed so shortly afterwards, to bear in mind what Pandurevic learned from Grujic and Bojanovic. In other words, that prisoners were being held in schools, in other words, not dead yet. And that Bojanovic told him that they were in buses on their way to Bijeljina which would have signalled to Pandurevic, Batkovic, and hence exchange and not murder at all. Unless there are any questions, those are my responses to your questions 2 and 3. I'm going to move on now to the appeal in relation to Pandurevic's failure to punish. In our submission, the Trial Chamber correctly found that Vinko Pandurevic discharged his duty to punish by writing the 15th of July and 18th of July reports and by his conversation with Krstic. At paragraph 2062, the Chamber articulated as follows: "Having considered all of the relevant evidence, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that in his 15th and 18th of July interim combat reports were a means, potentially the only such realistic available means, for Pandurevic to communicate and report to the competent authorities about the crimes that were committed in the Zvornik area." The Trial Chamber also recalls that Pandurevic raised the issue of the execution of prisoners in Zvornik with Krstic in person on the 27th of July, specifically Pandurevic asked Krstic if he had any more specific information about the matter, to which Krstic responded that it was not something that should be Pandurevic's concern and that he, Krstic, would deal with the problem in the appropriate way. The Prosecution challenged that finding by arguing that the Trial Chamber added an element to the legal standard requiring for the measures to be necessary, reasonable, and certain to be effective. That is not what the Trial Chamber did. The correct standard, reasonable and necessary measures means the availability of measures has to be assessed on the basis of the circumstances surrounding each particular situation. And that's the Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 417. "Reasonable" means measures reasonably falling within the material powers, not a question of substantive law but of evidence, according to the Appeals Chamber in Halilovic, paragraph 63. Pandurevic's material ability needs to be assessed, taking into consideration the circumstances at the time. An abstract listing of all the measures the Prosecution can think about now, some of which were not even litigated during trial, is not the proper legal standard. This brings me to question 4, the military prosecutor and other measures. The Trial Chamber reasonably found that Pandurevic had taken the only necessary and reasonable measures he could. This question, Your Honours, cannot be divorced from reality. It has to bear upon the circumstances in which the commander found himself, and I may reach slightly outside this case and this courtroom for just a moment, but let us take a look around ourselves. Karadzic is being tried down the corridor for offences relating to the events of Srebrenica. Mladic is being tried downstairs in relation to events concerning Srebrenica. Beara, Tolimir, Miletic, Gvero, the whole Main Staff were involved in the events at Srebrenica. By the 27th of July, when he visited Krstic, indeed by the 23rd of July, when he spoke to Dragan Obrenovic, and I particularly invite you to consider paragraph 1910 about that conversation, Pandurevic was rightly aware that the whole of the Main Staff was involved in these events. If he were here today offering up the fact that he had reported his concerns to the military prosecutor, an organ of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Prosecution would laugh at him and suggest that such a measure was wholly inadequate to discharge his duties as a commander. They would say that reporting this matter to the military prosecutor was mere window dressing. It's worthy of note that during the many days he cross-examined Vinko Pandurevic, Peter McCloskey never once suggested to him that that was an option he should have chosen. Moreover, during the trial, the Prosecution did not find it important enough to present evidence on the military prosecutor, that's at the trial judgement paragraph 2057, and the evidence that was presented mentioned by Mr. Wood this morning was only suggestive of its impartiality. In our submission, the Trial Chamber rightly looked at all the options available to Pandurevic and decided that in the writing of reports to his immediate superior and by personally visiting his immediate superior he had taken all necessary, appropriate measures. That was a considered and intelligent reflection upon the position he realistically found himself in. We addressed the other points suggested or the other measures suggested he might have taken regarding investigations and disciplinary measures in our response brief at paragraphs 256 to 269, and I will not and I doubt I have the time to go through them now. It remains our position that the 15th and 18th of July reports, as well as the conversation with Krstic, were the only reasonable and necessary measures he could have taken. They created a written record, higher command who were informed could deal with his superiors as well as his subordinates. As for our position on question 5 which you've posed us, the reports of the 15th and the 18th of July invite an inquiry which is not in fact limited in time. So the question whether he can be found liable for failing to punish the crimes committed before he returned to Zvornik is moot because it is our case that the Trial Chamber correctly considered that he had discharged that duty in relation to both the crimes before and after his return. For what it is worth, we take no position on the question as to whether as a matter of principle Pandurevic could be liable for failing to punish those crimes which occurred between the 13th and the 15th of July, when we say he was not in command of the brigade. We note that in the Prosecution's submissions this morning as to the relevant law on this topic, the one case they didn't make reference to was that of Perisic, where the same legal standard was applied and the Prosecution did not express the view that they expressed here this morning, with the necessary effect that Perisic was acquitted. I'm coming to the end. Paragraph 2209 of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber acknowledged the uncommon and extraordinary set of facts that set aside the case of Vinko Pandurevic. One of its uncommon and extraordinary features is the narrative I've described for you, whereby a young commander doing, as the Trial Chamber found, the work of a soldier properly, returned to his headquarters to be told that others had brought into what is termed his zone of responsibility a lot of prisoners and they were going about killing them. As you know, I did not address you about Vinko Pandurevic's sentence. The Prosecution have done so today and invoked the rights of victims. I wholly support the rights of victims, as does Vinko Pandurevic, to whom the Trial Chamber in this instance found to have performed a compelling act of assistance in July of 1995. One of the principal rights of victims is the right to truth, and for all the rhetoric about the digger drivers and guards who in a formal sense might have been Pandurevic's subordinates and who might have aided and abetted unbeknown to him the scheme to murder people, the Prosecution have repeatedly denied the victims of Srebrenica this right. But perhaps they'll do so in a reply today. We know that a few soldiers from the 1st Battalion went to the Kula school to stand guard, but who was in charge there? Who ordered the shootings to start? And at Petkovci, who was in charge on the ground? Who ordered the killings to begin? And at Orahovac and at Kula? The answer to that central question has always born and continues to bear on every level of Pandurevic's culpability and sentence. Unless you have any questions to ask of me, those are the submissions I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll now have the Prosecution's reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'll just make some brief remarks on -- in reply on all of the submissions other than those made on behalf of Mr. Nikolic, and my colleague, Mr. Rogers, will reply to those. I want to start by very quickly dealing with the Popovic and Beara comments in relation to the cumulative conviction for conspiracy to commit genocide responses, and I have no comments on Mr. Popovic's response. But in respect of Mr. Beara my invitation to you is that you should ignore his response as non-responsive. He does not address the legal issue raised in the ground or in the submissions. What he used the opportunity to do was to rehash his appellant's argument and challenge the underlying factual findings on conspiracy to commit genocide, and in our respectful submission that was improper. And I note that - and Your Honours are probably well aware of this - that Beara did not file a response to the Prosecutor's -- Prosecution appeal brief and, as such, his response on paper, at least, again is not available to you for any purpose that would serve you in terms of deciding this legal issue that has been decided by the Appeals Chamber of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. In terms of Miletic, I have no comment, given the concession by Ms. Faveau on this legal issue, and so I will turn to Mr. Pandurevic. The submissions on grounds 1 and grounds 2 are interesting but generally non-responsive because Mr. Pandurevic's counsel avoided the central issue put forward by the Prosecution as the basis for the error in 1972 and 1973 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. And that is, in considering Vinko Pandurevic's shared intent for the joint criminal enterprise to murder, the Trial Chamber ignored its own findings, particularly the findings in relation to the words used and the meaning that it derived from and found from the 15th July interim combat report. Mr. Haynes avoids the question and it's been a question that I think vexes him because the Trial Chamber did, in fact, spend a lot of time analysing the evidence and making those findings so that our position is, quite clearly, that there is a legal error, a legal error that compels this Appeals Chamber to look at the findings and look at the facts and make your own determination to see what the proper conclusion would have been had the findings in 1948 been applied and the contextual circumstances been used to do that evaluation. We have -- in our submissions today and in our Prosecution appeal brief and reply we have tried to help the Trial Chamber -- or the Appeals Chamber in evaluating whether or not this ground of appeal is factually and legally founded and also to provide you with ample references to the trial record to assist you in making the determination that we suggest, with respect, you should be making. The standard of review put forward by Mr. Pandurevic's counsel in our submission is wrong. It essentially suggests that if there is a dissenting opinion then there is no possibility to make a determination that no reasonable Trial Chamber could make that conclusion. Our position is that this Appeals Chamber on a regular basis applies the standard of review for appeals, and I won't tell you what the law is. You know it and you apply it regularly. And this Appeals Chamber is not afraid to take on the difficult and challenging job of reviewing factual findings and evidence and replacing its findings on facts and guilt or innocence in place of decisions made by Trial Chambers. The emphasis in the response by Pandurevic is on the conversation of Obrenovic and Grujic, but again without addressing the problem that it create -- that is created by the 15th July ICR which suggests, as found by the Trial Chamber, that Pandurevic in fact held much more knowledge when looked at in the context of the conversations and the document. During the course of his remarks, he made one submission relating to prisoners and that prisoners were regularly exchanged from the 20th to the 24th of July. I note to remind you of the fact that he has been convicted for the aiding and abetting of murder of the ten patients from the Milici hospital that were turned over to Popovic that you've heard about in the proceedings, and I also refer you to paragraph 59 of our reply, where we address this specific point in response -- in reply to his response. I can just simply repeat for Your Honours that we did in our brief set out the basics of the legal and factual position of the Prosecution and why an appeal on these two grounds should be allowed. And Mr. Haynes, on behalf of Mr. Pandurevic, has replied -- responded in full. The arguments that he advances this morning on these grounds add little, if anything, to what he says in his response. And we have addressed any points that are worth responding -- responding to in our replies, and, consequently, I will rely on your study of the response and reply and not bore you anymore this afternoon. I'll pass the podium on to Mr. Rogers for a brief reply in respect of the Nikolic points - thank you, Your Honours - unless there are some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have three points I wish to make in reply to the submissions of my learned friend for Drago Nikolic. The first relates to his assertions concerning withdrawal or extraction. Your Honours, I want to address that suggestion that he withdrew from the enterprise, that's Drago Nikolic withdrew. My learned friend at transcript 64 said: The Trial Chamber considered the limited scope of his acts and his withdrawal from the criminal acts prior to their completion and he referred to the judgement at 1410. But, Your Honours, this might imply that the Trial Chamber considered that Drago Nikolic had made some positive decision to withdraw or, as my learned friend put it later in the transcript at 74, that Drago Nikolic was nonetheless able to extract himself at the earliest opportunity. But if we examine the judgement at 1410, we see what they said. They said: "His participation in the killing operation is limited in time beginning on the night of 13 and ending suddenly midday on 16 July. As a result, he is not directly implicated in the killings at Branjevo Military Farm or Pilica cultural centre." In our submission, that is not an extraction or a withdrawal. This was not the Trial Chamber's impression of him at all. What they said when considering his responsibility in relation to the joint criminal enterprise to murder at paragraph 1392 was this: "He played an important role in the organisation of the operation by which the common purpose was achieved and he made a number of contributions to that common purpose through his work, behind the scenes of and at various detention and execution sites in Zvornik. Notably, he arranged for personnel to guard and carry out executions and was personally present at Orahovac in an organisational capacity at the detention and execution sites at times when the executions were being carried out. Through these acts, he made a significant contribution and from his steadfast and resolute approach to the task given to him in the murder operation, it is clear that he shared the intent of the common purpose." Your Honours, the second that I wish to address is the comments relating to Drago Nikolic's belief about the prisoners. At transcript page 64, my learned friend referred to Drago Nikolic witnessing the targeting of the Bosnian Muslims and said that: "The Trial Chamber considered Drago Nikolic's belief that prisoners as opposed to any other description of victims were being brought in to the Zvornik area." And he referred to the judgement at 1402-1403. However, Your Honours, this reference should not be misunderstood to indicate that Drago Nikolic only thought that prisoners were prisoners of war.
