The Trial Chamber referred to Drago Nikolic's knowledge when he left the Standard Barracks on the morning of the 14th of July, in judgement 1404, when it stated: "The only reasonable inference to draw from such a planning meeting is that when he leaves Standard Barracks that morning, he knows the details of the plan, the executions were to be carried out in multiple locations in the Zvornik area, and the victims would number in the hundreds to thousands. Later that morning, he sees the convoy of buses, and, subsequently, he acquires first-hand information from his observations at Orahovac about the composition of the victims, soldiers and civilians, men, boys, and elderly. It was also apparent that these unarmed weakened Bosnian Muslim males already in VRS custody constituted no military threat." Finally, I wish to address my learned friend's remarks concerning contextual knowledge. At the transcript at page 72 of today's hearing, my learned friend stated that contextual knowledge refers to the full spectrum of the knowledge of the accused which necessarily has a bearing on his understanding of the situation and accordingly on his actions. Your Honours, I'd like to address you and take you to some of the judgement findings referring to the broad spectrum of that knowledge to contextualise it. In the judgement at 1418, dealing with the knowledge requirements under Article 5, the Trial Chamber found that: "Nikolic, as chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade, whose commander took part in the attack on Srebrenica, knew of the military attack against the protected Srebrenica enclave. He further knew that the Bosnian Muslim prisoners were transported from Bratunac to Zvornik, therefore he knew that these were prisoners who had come into the custody of the VRS as a result of the attack on the civilian enclave of Srebrenica. Nikolic saw that the Bosnian Muslim prisoners detained at the Grbavci school and executed at Orahovac were not only soldiers but also civilians and that no distinction or selection was made in terms of those to be executed. Nikolic's acts of murder are clearly tied to the attack on Srebrenica and Nikolic knew that this was the case." Concerning their findings relating to extermination, the Trial Chamber found that these murders were either within the common purpose of the JCE to murder or were a natural and foreseeable consequence of it. Nikolic participated in the JCE to murder and he also ordered and planned murder as a crime against humanity. These murders, to Nikolic's knowledge, were carried out on a massive scale with thousands of victims; thus Nikolic committed, ordered, and planned murder on a large scale. On the basis of these combined circumstances, the Trial Chamber finds Nikolic guilty of extermination. And the circumstances are further confirmed in their full context in the Trial Chamber's judgement at paragraph 1426 concerning persecution. They found: "Nikolic participated in the killing operation with the specific intent to discriminate on political, racial, or religious grounds. The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that Nikolic's involvement in the organisation and co-ordination of the massive-scale murder of a single ethnic group, the Bosnian Muslims, shows his discriminatory intent. Moreover, his active participation in the detention, killing, and reburial, the circumstances and manner of which plainly display discriminatory intent as previously found by the Trial Chamber is further proof of Nikolic's intent. The Trial Chamber therefore finds that Nikolic participated in the JCE to murder with specific intent to discriminate on political, racial, or religious grounds, and thereby committed persecution through murder and cruel and inhumane treatment." Your Honours, those are the full contextual circumstances of Drago Nikolic's acts. Your Honours, we have no further submissions unless we can help you any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, okay, we'll take the break now and return at 20 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We come now to the personal addresses by the appellants, and I advise all the appellants that they have a right, if they wish to exercise it, to make an address. Mr. Popovic, do you wish to make an address? The address is not to exceed ten minutes. THE APPELLANT POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It is my intention to do so and I know that I have ten minutes. Can I begin, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please do. THE APPELLANT POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, it is not my intention to repeat what was said in either my appeal or my judgement. I just wish to point out some facts that I noticed. I would like to say that I never even thought of eliminating a group or part of a group belonging to the opposing side. I never commanded, ordered, or made it possible for anybody to be killed. During the conflict, I never commanded a combat unit. I did not notice that it was the plan of my superiors to commit genocide or kill anybody. Your Honours, is it possible that the genocide at Srebrenica was committed by three security officers of whom I am one? On the other hand, 14 persons have been tried here, of whom many were commanders, which means that they exercised command duties in whose area of responsibility crimes were committed and genocide by using their resources and yet nobody was convicted of genocide. It is observed that according to the findings of this Tribunal, I was assisted in genocide by my commander, Krstic. In this courtroom Article 17 of the temporary regulations of the VRS was shown, but it was not correctly explained. Your Honours, an officer from the superior command cannot come without any authorisation and do what he pleases, as has been said, without a verification. If he has a written authorisation, that's all right, but if he doesn't then he must be verified by the superior officer in his own unit and in the superior command. They must be informed. And as for using the resources of a unit for which the commander and the crews can be held criminally responsible, namely, engaging manpower, using fuel, ammunition, machinery, and equipment, I can say that I haven't had any conversations with Momir Nikolic by any means, although this was -- this is contained in the judgement. I never talked to Drago Nikolic about the entry of prisoners of war at Zvornik. I didn't assist or wasn't present at any execution at Orahovac, and I saw Acimovic for the first time in this courtroom. I didn't take the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to Branjevo, and I have never been at Branjevo, especially not at the time of the execution. That people from Milici were members of the Zvornik Brigade, I heard of them first -- for the first time here. Please pay attention to P1309. Your Honours, this intercept cannot establish a link between the wounded at Milici and this. The commander says: I have prisoners, I have injured men. But of course after such a fierce combat it is not possible to take prisoner only healthy men. Of course there are wounded people. And then there was the letter: Should I send the wounded to the Zvornik hospital? What would be the point of sending the wounded from Milici to the Zvornik hospital when they already had been there? And thirdly, there are no entries in the log-book that I stayed at the brigade at Zvornik on that day at all. And fourthly, these people mentioned here were exchanged and I am still not familiar with the fate of the wounded from Milici to this day. Now let me say why the evidence has been so twisted. All -- everybody was at the Tribunal at the same time, Krstic, Obrenovic, Jokic, Blagojevic, Momir Nikolic, some were politicians, some were servicemen. Of course they had at their disposal evidence and everything that incriminated them. They had time to think of how they could shift the blame to somebody else. The system of the empty chair was used. The character of this judgement is such that to my mind all evidence was twisted in the worst possible manner. Where nobody recognised me, the Trial Chamber did. When it was a person with a moustache, it was me. When it was a person without a moustache, it was me again. If he was tall with greyish hair, about 50 years old, it was me. If he was standing beside a Kampanjola vehicle, it was again me. If he was driving a Golf, of course it was me. A description was made which didn't fit me at all, but it was me. On a number of occasions I must have been at two places at the same time, Dragasevac and Kozluk, for example, Kozluk and Nis, Orahovac and Krivaca, although the distance is from 60 to 80 kilometres. Then how can I defend myself? Half truths and lies were used here. Words were taken out of context and all the evidence of the Defence was neglected and different standards were applied to the Defence and to the Prosecution. In not one case was the principle of favouring the defendant applied. If the purpose was to convict me at all costs, then the Trial Chamber surely achieved its goal and the red square shown by -- but then the red square shown by the Prosecutor would not have been red, there would have been an interruption in the line of command. But the line of command is one thing and the professional lines are something else. And let me finish by saying that I appeal to you to use both ears in your heads. Thank you for listening to me. May I sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may, and I thank you for your statement. Mr. Beara, do you wish to make a statement? THE APPELLANT BEARA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for offering me to make a statement, but I have nothing to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Nikolic, do you wish to make a statement? THE APPELLANT NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, for the second time I have the opportunity now to address you. I did so at the end of my trial, and I can say without any hesitation that what I said back then really helped me to cope with all these events. Today that all the proceedings have come to an end, there are many things I would like to say, but I am not a man of many words and it has never been easy for me to show my feelings. That's why I'll be brief. At the very start I would like to thank my Defence counsel and my Defence team. It has been eight years now since they began to work with me, and irrespective of the final outcome I wish to say thank you. Not only did my attorneys help me a lot, but working with them I learned a lot about myself too. Likewise, I would like to express my gratitude to the witnesses who came to witness -- who came to testify in my defence, and many did so jeopardising themselves although they didn't even know me. Of course I was not satisfied with the judgement, which in many respects was surprising. I really hope that the submissions made this week have convinced you that what is described in the judgement is not what actually happened. However, regardless of the outcome and the sentence that I will receive in the end, I must tell you what weighs heaviest on my mind, namely, that I'm simply not the man described in the judgment. My attorneys explained to me that whatever I say today will not affect my proceedings in any way because I did not testify, and yet I wish to say at least for those who are following this trial -- these proceedings that I didn't know about the prisoners arriving in Orahovac until the late evening of the 13th of July and until I was summoned to the meeting with Beara and Popovic on the following day. When I met with them, I was not informed that the prisoners would be killed. It was a very short meeting, during which I was informed that for security reasons a great group of prisoners would arrive at Bratunac and that they will be put up at different schools in the area to be exchanged. To my mind, it was a crazy idea because of the security risk to the population. And only later when armed people unknown to me arrived at Orahovac, I realised that the prisoners would be killed. From that moment on I focused on two things: I wanted to protect the young members of the military police from my brigade from being involved in that nightmare and I wanted to protect myself, for which I deeply regret. There were conditions for me to do more, in spite of my low rank and my lack of influence, and I am paying a heavy price today for this grave mistake. I wish this had never happened and I'm truly sorry that all these people were killed. No matter how we look at that war, such a tragedy cannot be justified. And finally, I wish to say that from my arrival to the Netherlands more than eight years ago, I was well treated by the guards at the Detention Unit and that all Judges and attorneys treated me with respect, for which I am grateful to them. At this moment I really am unable to say anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Pandurevic. THE APPELLANT PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at trial I used the opportunity to testify for 22 days in public session and without any protective measures. I did not hesitate to answer every single question. I described the events that were relevant to the area and time covered by the indictment. I did so fully, honestly, and with the best of intentions. I think that my testimony was the best way to address the Chamber and tell them what I knew; however, Your Honour, I also appreciate highly this opportunity to address you here. My career as an officer who graduated from the military academy started in Slovenia, where I stayed when the war broke out. This was a war that the JNA officers were not ready for and had not been preparing for. The whirlwind of the war took me from Slovenia across Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war was even more cruel, just as any civil war is, yet another war that we weren't prepared for. I was always guided by the values that were given to me by my family and my father who always said: Do not look beyond the fence into the neighbour's yard; rather, live as best you can. And I did so during the war, treating others humanely, assisting the enemy as far as the laws of war and human ethics dictated. As an officer, I went through various training courses, such as the one in Ljubljana, where I got a master's degree in social studies, and I attended other courses that had to do with the social sciences in the army. I had various duties including that of an assistant professor at the University of Sarajevo. All the duties in the army were command duties from the battalion commander to the brigade commander, as well as the duties of the deputy commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. As you know, Your Honour, I'm the only accused in this case -- and I was the one who fully experienced the command responsibility in the war. Addressing the issue of command responsibility is a sensitive thing. One has to approach it from one's own view of ethics. To discuss command responsibility, or rather, in the US army military view, for the months of January/February 2012, there is a critical view of the fact that the -- commanders are responsible for everything that their subordinates may do. [In English] A commander is responsible but very often not in control. [Interpretation] An army is a human organisation where, unfortunately, bad things happen. One cannot anticipate them and know how to react. When chaos emerges, the commander needs to take decisions. In terms of organisation, we cannot expect the commander to bear responsibility for all the criminal actions on the part of his subordinates unless he was aware of and ignored these circumstances or engaged in activities that were conducive to such criminal acts. The VRS was a people's army, and the commander was unable to supervise and manage one 's units 24 hours a day, seven days a week. This was impossible. To control a brigade is not the same as controlling a crew on the ship. The commander cannot keep tabs on all the bad things; however, the commander is responsible for creating -- [In English] A commander is responsible but very often not in control. [Interpretation] In the period between 4 and 15 July, I was absent from the AOR of the brigade. I was in command of a different unit and had no effective control over the Zvornik Brigade. In that period, I did not receive a single report from the Zvornik Brigade nor did I issue a single order to the Zvornik Brigade. As is well-known, Your Honours, after the capture of the members of the 28th Division of the BH army, some of them were transported to the Zvornik municipality and were then executed. These prisoners of war were not within the AOR or responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. The execution of these soldiers in the Zvornik municipality was a deed of individuals who were not members of the Zvornik Brigade but of other structures of the VRS. These criminal activities did include some members of the Zvornik Brigade; however, they did not do so under my order, approval, or tacit approval as brigade commander. The Trial Chamber was not able to come across a single illegal order that I would have issued in relation to the prisoners of war. As a former member of the VRS and as a human being, I condemn most strongly all these crimes and express my commiseration with the victims. The members of the 28th Division who were captured by the members of the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995 were prisoners of war in the custody of the Zvornik Brigade. They survived and they were treated in accordance with the international humanitarian law regulations. They were sent to the Batkovic camp near Bijeljina and were later exchanged. There were 145 of them. As His Honour Judge Kwon put it, I was the only one who did not stay silent about any of the events that happened in the territory of the Zvornik Brigade; rather, I noted down all these events in my regular and interim combat reports as information came to me. This is the only official information in the VRS documentation mentioning the execution of the prisoners. The information that I noted down in my reports was not further conveyed in other reports. My interim command report that I issued on the 18th of July and sent to the Drina Corps shows what I knew of the prisoners executed in the Zvornik Brigade. These reports, in addition to my oral reports, constitute my legal duty to report to my superior of the illegal events in my AOR. It was impossible or quite something that I was not able to do, that's to say to try and have those who committed these crimes punished because they were not within my AOR. I was also there to release the column by opening up the corridor. Your Honour, I think as brigade commander under those circumstances I did act within the remit of my duty as commander and I did as was right. As I did back then, I do now condemn the fact that these crimes happened and I apologise on my behalf and on behalf of the Zvornik Brigade to all the victims and their families. I thank you, Your Honours. I thank the Prosecution and especially my Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic says there's an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I noticed -- I noticed an error in transcript. It is on the page 104, lines 16 and 17, it reads -- these are Mr. Popovic's words: "I saw Drago Nikolic for the first time in this courtroom ..." The name "Drago Nikolic" is the error because Mr. Popovic said: I saw Srecko Acimovic for the first time in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, the correction will be made. I'm sorry, you have a comment on that, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, it's a different topic, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, because we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- which has to do with what Mr. Nikolic told the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said we are now going to hear from Mr. Miletic who has asked that his personal statement be read by his counsel. Counsel, you may read his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to read Mr. Miletic's statement in the language he has written the statement, i.e., in Serbo-Croatian. Your Honours, anything that I may have to say about the judgement and the assessment of evidence or the way the Trial Chamber proceeded would be superfluous. I am certain that through the evidence presented by my Defence team you were able to arrive at all the relevant information related to me personally and the position I had during the war in the former Yugoslavia. Primarily, I'm referring to my duty in the staff sector of the Main Staff which did not have any de facto or de jure command authority outside of the administration for operations and training and outside of the south sector when the Chief of Staff was absent from the command post. None of the commands of the former JNA or the VRS had within its establishment the role of adviser. It turns out here that my immediate superiors included both the Chief of Staff as my immediate superior and the commander who was my superior second in the line and was the immediate superior of the Chief of Staff. Under the law, the rules of engagement and instructions, this is impermissible and impossible and contrary to the establishment of the Main Staff. Unlike the Chief of Staff and the assistant commander who had command authority over specific units, I did not have any subordinate units and I could only ever issue direct orders to the senior officers from the administration for operations and training. None of my subordinates or myself, for that matter, were ever seen in Srebrenica or Zepa in July 1995. It is an exclusive right of the commander in all the armies across the world to make decisions and in this way express his intention as to the way in which he wishes to reach the objective, and nobody else within the command has that right and especially not the chief of the administration for operations and training. In principle, where the commander is that is where the command is. Nobody has the right, nor would the commander allow for that, to co-ordinate the work of the commander and his subordinates. Nobody can be more informed about the situation in the battle-field where the commander is present than the commander himself, and this was what the Trial Chamber erred in. Co-ordination implies co-ordination and management, and senior officers can exercise co-ordination only pursuant to a written order from the commander of the Main Staff. My role within the drafting of the directive was regulated in precise terms in the instructions for the work of the commands and staffs and annexes, paragraphs 95 to 140 and 95 to 103, where it is stated where decisions are made within a team, this is what the role of the operations officer will be in drafting the directive. The operations officer will draft the plan according to which the commander will work and take decisions pursuant to the order and instructions from the commander or the Chief of Staff. He will also assess own forces and the terrain and make an assessment of the time and will make an assessment for the Chief of Staff to draw conclusions from. Further duties of the operations organ until the -- a decision is taken includes noting down or recording proposals given by the Chief of Staff or the tasks that the Chief of Staff may have for the units and command and control and will also write down the proposals from the assistant commander -- from assistant commanders within their professional lines of duty. Thereafter, the commander himself will make his decision known by either adopting these proposals fully or partly or making his own decision. The commander will then issue a task to the Chief of Staff and other members of the team who are then to formulate sections of the directive from their own purview and send them to the operations officer. The chief of the operations sector will then put the directive together and would put the various proposals into the various sections so that they, the directive itself, would have the proper shape and form. In keeping with paragraphs 103.3, 493, 502, and 504 of the instructions governing the work of commands and staffs. The operations sector has the duty to compile and draft the directive on the basis of the proposals received without amending it or modifying it in any way and submit it to the Chief of Staff, who will review the draft and send it on to the commander. This is the way the Directive 7 and 7.1 were drafted. At the meeting of the commanders which took place on the 3rd of March, 1995, which is noted down in the commander's diary, the commander took the decision and I drafted the directive according to the said method. The directive and the disk on which the directive was recorded were handed over on the 4th of March, 1995, to the Chief of Staff who was supposed to read it and send it on to the commander. And this is how things happened because both I and the Chief of Staff were away from the Main Staff in the days that followed. The directive was produced on a computer. It is hard for me, therefore, to understand why there is no pagination on the first and last page and why the last line on page 10 should be repeated on -- as the first line on page 11. I could not have made such a mistake because Milovanovic would have spotted it and returned the directive to me. Normally he never would miss such mistakes. I would like to draw your attention to a couple of details about myself as a human being, officer in general. I have been in detention for eight years now and I have been socialising with the detainees of all ethnicities and I have never had the slightest of problems with that. I was born in a mixed village in Eastern Bosnia. The whole family of mine is multi-ethnic. My wife is a Croat and our convictions that religion and ethnicity do not matter is something that we have transferred to our children. My son is also married to a Croat and my daughter is married to a Macedonian. We believe that multi-culturality is -- in the family is our enormous wealth. Religion, ethnicity, or the colour of the skin have never been the parameters based on which we would judge people. In the beginning of the war, my two friends, one of them Zeljko, a Croat, and Muharem, a Muslim, risked their lives to help me pull out of Sarajevo the families of my brother and sister. As a young man I lived in Sarajevo and I cannot even begin to describe how sad I was when I had to leave it in 1967 for Zadar and it was even harder for me to see what was happening to Sarajevo during the war. I am 100 per cent sure that I and most of the senior officers of all ethnicities did not wish for the war to happen. We knew what war meant, unlike many of the hot heads who had no idea what they were doing. The war did not bring any good to people, only innocent victims, destroyed homes, and devastated families. My value judgement is such that there can be no justification for a crime. I am certain about what I am and what I did. I was honourable -- I was an honourable soldier and a general, and primarily as a human being I can say that my conscience is clear and I can look everybody in their eye. An honourable and honest man has nothing to be ashamed of. Now, what is important here are victims, victims that do not have a colour of the skin, religion, or ethnicity. They are simply innocent victims, and, as such, deserve that the truth be heard of their fate. I want to pay my respects and my condolences to their families. I did not have the intention of contributing to the tragic fate of any person through action or inaction. I went through life doing an honest job of work and caring for my family. That's why I volunteered as soon as the indictment was published on the 15th of February, 2005, because I believed that an innocent man has nothing to fear. I volunteered to come before this Court. Your Honour, thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you in this way and for your patience in hearing me out. Radivoje Miletic, Scheveningen, 6 December 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave, I'd like to address quickly the Chamber. Maybe it would be better if Mr. Nikolic could remove his earphones, Mr. President, because it has to do with something that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a strange request.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's -- the reason, Mr. President, is that he informed us before what he would say and there's something in the transcript that took us by surprise and we don't know if it was said either in English or in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I've consulted with my sister and brothers and we will not accede to the request. I turn now to the last matter, the next Status Conference in this case is due to be held on or before the 22nd of December, 2013, and I consider it wise to address the issues that would arise in such a conference. Currently the Appeals Chamber is seized of seven motions, which are all under consideration and the decisions will be issued in due course. Now, prior to adjourning I'd like to ask each of the appellants whether they wish to raise any concerns regarding their health or the conditions of their detention. Mr. Popovic, do you have any matters that you wish to raise? THE APPELLANT POPOVIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Everything is all right for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Beara? THE APPELLANT BEARA: [Interpretation] Everything is the way it should be. Thank you. I have no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic. THE APPELLANT NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no problems. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pandurevic. THE APPELLANT PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the conditions are good and everything is in line with the regulations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And are there any additional matters to be raised by the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Not by the Prosecution, but I note that Ms. Faveau has not spoken on behalf of her client. She may want to offer --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: No, no, vis-a-vis his health and the conditions of detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Faveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we go in closed session or private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, any other matters to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I respect the decision that you took a minute ago with regard to the submission of Mr. Bourgon, but I kindly ask you to allow us to have the transcript corrected subsequently because I heard what Mr. Nikolic said but it was recorded differently. And we will try to correct the transcript if you allow. Page 107, lines 18 through 23, are the reference in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reminded that there is in place a Registry procedure for the verification of the transcript, and I advise that you follow that. This concludes the hearing of the appeals. I'd like to thank on behalf of the Chamber the parties for their submissions, I'd also like to express my gratitude to the interpreters, the court reporters, the court officers, the court ushers, the audio/visual staff, IT, security, and all staff involved for their assistance and co-operation during this week. The Chamber will issue its judgement in due course. We are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.24 p.m.
